#6215. The Airbus A350's Cockpit Actually Shares Its DNA With The World's Largest Passenger Jet

The Airbus A380 may be disappearing from airline fleets, but one of its most important ideas is still sitting in front of pilots every time an A350 leaves the ground. The connection is easy to miss because the A350 flight deck does not look like a smaller version of the superjumbo's cockpit. Its six large displays, different control system, and cleaner layout make it look like a newer generation altogether. Basically, Airbus deliberately started with the A380 concept and carried several of its most important ideas into the A350.

That makes the interesting question less about whether the A350 copied the A380 and more about what Airbus kept, what it changed, and why. The answer can be found in the displays, the way pilots interact with them, the avionics architecture underneath and, ultimately, the amount of training an airline can avoid when moving crews between Airbus types. The A350’s cockpit is the result of what Airbus did with the A380's cockpit lessons once it had a smaller, more efficient aircraft to design.

The family connection is not just an impression created by similar flight-control philosophy. Airbus says the A350 cockpit was designed with its cockpit philosophy in mind, while its dedicated A350 technical material describes the A380 cockpit as the starting point for the newer flight deck. The company then added larger screens, better positioning, and more interaction between pilots. Airbus' A350 cockpit material is unusually clear on that point.

The timeline explains the evolution well. The A380 entered service in 2007, giving Airbus several years of operational experience with a highly integrated widebody flight deck before the A350 made its first flight in June 2013. The A350-900 then entered commercial service with Qatar Airways in January 2015. By then, Airbus had a useful opportunity: it could take ideas already introduced on the A380 and redesign the interface instead of simply reproducing it.

The avionics suppliers were working along the same path. Aviation Today reported back in 2009 that several A350 avionics systems were being developed as a technology continuum from the A380, with common hardware and software baselines intended to help systems mature sooner. Honeywell, for example, said it would retain the A380 hardware and baseline software for systems such as flight management and aircraft environment surveillance, while focusing A350-specific development on software and new functions.

That continuity did not mean Airbus stopped experimenting. You notice it right away: the A350 has fewer displays, but each one can do more. That is where the A380's cockpit concept becomes the A350's own design.

The biggest visual difference is also one of the clearest signs that Airbus refined rather than copied and pasted its earlier design. The A380 has eight main flight-deck displays, plus additional screens for its Onboard Information System. The A350 instead uses six identical large-format displays. Airbus says that all six share the same part number and are fully interchangeable in hardware and software.

That uniformity changes how the cockpit behaves. On the A350, information can be rearranged across the flight deck instead of being tied as closely to a particular physical screen. Airbus' own technical description explains that the Onboard Information System can be placed on a central display, allowing pilots to share information more easily during a briefing. If a display fails, the system can automatically reconfigure the avionics pages, while information from an outer-screen failure can be recovered elsewhere.

The result is a cockpit that is less about memorizing where a particular page lives and more about deciding which information should be visible at a particular moment. Leeham News highlighted the same principle in its comparison of the A350 with earlier Airbus flight decks.

Smaller changes matter too. The primary flight display adds information such as flap and trim indications below the main presentation, while the navigation display can provide a vertical profile of the route and terrain. The thrust presentation also follows the simplified percentage-based philosophy introduced with the A380 rather than returning to the older split between N1 and EPR indications.

The six-screen arrangement solves a problem created by the older cockpit philosophy: if the screen is no longer the boundary, the pilot needs a better way to control whatever appears on it. That led Airbus to change the interface itself.

Ten classic airliners relied on a third cockpit crew member, but their reasons for doing so reveal how dramatically commercial aviation evolved.

The A350's Keyboard and Cursor Control Units, or KCCUs, are one of the least obvious but most important departures from older Airbus cockpits. Instead of each pilot being tied to a Multifunction Control and Display Unit with its own small screen, the KCCU lets the crew interact with the larger cockpit displays.

Leeham News described the difference in practical terms: the older MCDU largely controls the information on its own display, while the A350's KCCU can control the wider flight deck. The cursor can move between fields and screens, making the system feel closer to a computer interface than the traditional scratchpad-and-enter workflow.

This is another case where the A380 provided the foundation. Airbus' A380 technical material shows that the superjumbo itself introduced KCCUs to control new functions, including its expanded avionics and information systems. The A350 took the concept further by making it central to a six-screen cockpit in which information could move around the flight deck.

Airbus subsequently added another layer. In December 2019, China Eastern Airlines received the first A350 equipped with the optional touchscreen cockpit displays. Airbus says three of the six displays can be touch-capable: the two outer screens and the lower-center display. The touchscreen interface complements, rather than replaces, the physical keyboard and KCCU.

However, the A350 did not suddenly become a flying game console that a flight sim can pilot without professional training. The touchscreen functions are integrated into a cockpit architecture that keeps the electronic flight bag separated from flight-critical avionics. Airbus' A350 technical documentation describes that separation explicitly, allowing airline applications to be used through the EFB without giving those applications a route into the aircraft's integrated avionics systems.

The same philosophy appears outside the screens. The A350 retains and develops functions first introduced on the A380, including the Onboard Airport Navigation System. During a Leeham News media flight, Fehrm used the airport map to select a runway exit and the Brake To Vacate function calculated an autobrake profile for the aircraft. A350 captain, Michele Scarton, also told Simple Flying that the aircraft's ground-navigation tools contribute to its ease of operation.

Once the interface is understood, the deeper connection becomes easier to see. The displays and KCCUs are the only parts pilots can touch. Underneath them is where Airbus carried the A380's architecture into a new generation.

The A350's Integrated Modular Avionics, or IMA, follows the same basic idea that made the A380's avionics architecture significant: multiple aircraft functions can share computing resources instead of relying on a separate physical box for every task.

Aviation Today described the A350 IMA platform as an evolution of the A380 architecture, with Thales supplying the core processing modules and Rockwell Collins providing the network switches. Airbus' later technical material describes further A350 improvements, including automatic reconfiguration intended to make certain low-criticality failures transparent to pilots.

The numbers illustrate the direction of travel. The A380 could host 23 flight-system functions on shared processing modules, while the A350's second-generation IMA can consolidate up to 40. The A350 also uses 18 data-network switches compared with 16 on the A380, according to the earlier Aviation Today material.

Airbus also carried forward the A380's move away from three hydraulic systems. The A380 uses two hydraulic and two electrical circuits, and the A350 refined the same 2H2E philosophy. The architecture is not identical, but the design logic is recognizably related: use electrical power and modular computing more aggressively while reducing conventional hardware elements.

This is the part of the A350 cockpit story that passengers never see. A screen layout can be changed in a redesign; the architecture underneath determines how systems are maintained, how failures are handled, and how much commonality an airline can exploit. That brings us back to why Airbus invested so heavily in cockpit family resemblance in the first place.

Airbus A330 vs A350: pilots reveal the real differences in cockpit design, aerodynamics, automation, and handling between the two Airbus widebodies

For an airline, cockpit commonality is useful only when it produces something measurable. In the A350's case, one of the biggest benefits is the training reduction when pilots already know another Airbus type.

Airbus says Cross Crew Qualification is available for A320 Family, A340 and A380 pilots, with training duration reduced by up to 78%. Its A350 commonality analysis also explains that A330 and A350 pilots can operate under a Common Type Rating arrangement based on the handling similarities between the aircraft.

The actual figures are useful because they show how far the family concept goes. As Simple Flying previously explored, the cross-crew qualification course takes 11 days for A320 Family pilots, 10 days for A340 pilots, and five days for A380 pilots. Airbus' current material adds that A330 pilots can qualify for the A350 without mandatory Full Flight Simulator time, with training time reduced by around 60% compared with a full type-rating course. The A380 figure is particularly revealing. The superjumbo's flight deck is the closest predecessor to the A350's, so pilots arriving from the A380 already understand much of the cockpit logic. But the A350 does not depend on A380 experience. Airbus designed it to preserve a wider Airbus commonality, which is why A330, A340, and A320 Family pilots can also transition through abbreviated training paths.

There is still a learning curve. For example, adapting to the A350's sidestick could take time for pilots accustomed to the conventional control column of older A300, A310, or Boeing aircraft. Commonality reduces the amount of new information a pilot has to absorb; it does not eliminate differences between aircraft.

For airlines operating several Airbus types, that distinction is important. A familiar cockpit can make it easier to roster crews, maintain multiple qualifications and reduce time away from line operations. Airbus explicitly links commonality to mixed-fleet flying and higher crew productivity. The A350 therefore turns cockpit design into an operational tool rather than an isolated piece of flight-deck ergonomics.

The A380's production ended with its final delivery in 2021, but the cockpit philosophy developed for the superjumbo has already moved on. The A350 is not an A380 flight deck copied onto a smaller airframe. It is what Airbus did with that experience once it had the opportunity to build a newer, lighter widebody around it. Simple Flying reported on the end of A380 production, but the more lasting story is what survived it.

That legacy will become easier to see as more A380 crews move onto newer Airbus aircraft. Qantas, for example, plans to begin retiring its A380s in fiscal year 2032 while introducing A350-1000s. Those pilots will not find identical cockpits, but the transition will still connect two generations of Airbus flight-deck design. The A380's physical cockpit may eventually disappear from airline service; much of its underlying logic will not.

That may ultimately be the more important legacy. Airbus is now pushing further toward software-defined aircraft, with its 2026 discussion of the concept pointing toward increasingly modular digital systems. The A380 was never the final word on the Airbus cockpit. It was a proving ground, and the A350 turned many of those ideas into a more practical design. The next generation will show just how far Airbus can take them.

#6214. Teamsters Sue Horizon Air Over Pilot Rest Rules

The Teamsters have sued Horizon Air, alleging the Alaska Air Group subsidiary violated federal labor law by changing how it handles pilots who report fatigue.

The Teamsters Airline Division and Local 1224 filed the lawsuit Oct. 23 in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington. The union alleges Horizon requires pilots who report fatigue at their home base to travel to another city as passengers before taking the rest provided under their contract.

The union alleges the practice violates the Railway Labor Act and is asking the court to order Horizon to stop it and restore the negotiated rest protections.

“Management cannot pick and choose which parts of our contract it wants to follow,” said Sean Lenney, a Horizon pilot and member of Local 1224, in a news release.

The Teamsters also said Thursday that 99% of pilots who voted backed a no-confidence measure against Carlos Zendejas, Horizon’s senior vice president of operations. The union’s Horizon Air Pilots Executive Council called for his removal following the vote.

Horizon and its pilots have been negotiating a new collective bargaining agreement for more than three and a half years, according to the union. Pilots held informational pickets in Seattle and Boise, Idaho, on Oct. 15 over issues including pay, staffing, and training.

#6213. How to Watch the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade

As the turkey thaws and a day of cooking prep begins, an equally integral Thanksgiving tradition is Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. Last year, 3.5 million spectators lined New York City’s streets to watch the procession of vibrant balloons and whimsical floats bob and weave through Midtown Manhattan to the beats of countless marching bands and celebrity performers. Beyond the city, a record-setting 34.3 million tuned into the NBC and Peacock broadcast, making the Emmy-winning production the year’s most-watched entertainment telecast. This year's promises to be even grander, as 2026 marks the 100th anniversary of the spectacle, which started in 1924 (though it wasn’t held from 1942 to 1944 because parade materials were reserved for wartime efforts).

“As a kid from the Bronx, it is an honor to bring this cherished tradition…to the city of New York every year,” the parade’s executive producer since 2021 Will Coss tells Condé Nast Traveler. The annual highlight for him is seeing the joyful expressions of spectators of all ages as the parade passes them by “showcasing some of the most iconic and recognizable pop culture characters and figures.”

This year marks the 99th anniversary of the Macy's Parade, an annual Thanksgiving tradition.

On the eve of the parade's centennial, the team—composed of painters, carpenters, animators, sculptures, welders, designers, engineers, and electricians—is honoring its past by way of revived classics like Felix the Cat and Underdog balloons. Ardent fans will also find a swath of newcomers that include a Fantasia-inspired Mickey, cowboy Minion, and a Peanuts duo. “The team at Macy’s Studios works year-round to make this historic parade bigger and better for our audiences every year,” Coss says. Here’s everything you need to know about the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in 2026—all its surprises, delights, and familiar joys.

When Macy’s first debuted its one-million-square foot New York City flagship store at 34th Street between Broadway and Seventh Avenues in 1924, the retailer threw a Christmas parade on Thanksgiving morning to boost holiday sales—with a much longer route starting at 145 Street and Covent Avenue. Balloons joined the lineup in 1927, starting with Felix the Cat, and the festivities were first broadcast nationally in 1947.

These days, the festive parade follows a 2.5-mile path from the Upper East Side to Midtown Manhattan. Starting at the corner of 77th Street and Central Park West, the route heads south to Columbus Circle and then turns east, heading along 59th Street to Sixth Avenue. From there, it goes straight down Sixth Avenue to 34th Street, ending in front of Macy’s flagship store in Herald Square.

Clifford the Big Red Dog in Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade.

Coss recommends arriving early for a great view. Many spectators start to gather as early as 6 a.m. along the beginning of the route on Central Park West (approach from the west) from 61st to 75th Streets. Other prime spots include the south side of 59th Street between Columbus Circle and Sixth Avenue and the entire stretch of Sixth Avenue between 38th and 59th. Spectators should be aware there is no viewing on Central Park West between 59th and 60th Streets, or anywhere south of 38th Street.

Coss also reminds those bringing children to dress warmly for the chilly weather and to be prepared to entertain young ones for a few hours while waiting to spot the first float. He suggests avoiding strollers, large bags, backpacks, and umbrellas.

In celebration of its centennial, some 100 inflatables will fly. Returning after decades are much-anticipated Felix the Cat (the parade's first character balloon, introduced in 1927) and Blue Hippopotamus (from the 1931 parade), while Hello Kitty and Underdog (who appeared in every parade from 1965 through 1984) will also make cameos. New to the scene are Bluey, Buckaroo Bob the Minion, and Snoopy persona Joe Cool with Woodstock, among others. The procession will also welcome 52 floats, 31 clown crews, nine specialty units (such as trycaloons, or balloons ridden on tricycles), seven marching bands, and five balloonicles (that’s a balloon-vehicle hybrid).

TODAY’s Savannah Guthrie, Hoda Kotb, and Al Roker will host the live broadcast of the 100th Macy’s Parade. Though this year's performance lineup has yet to be announced, the 2025 roster featured 26 celebrity performers, ranging from Colbie Caillat and Christopher Jackson to Foreigner and Taylor Momsen, complete with a performance by KPop Demon Hunters’ HUNTR/X singing voices EJAE, Audrey Nuna, and Rei Ami. As anticipation for the parade's centennial only increases, Coss says this year will “bring new surprises and delights to the iconic holiday tradition and truly celebrate this incredibly special anniversary.”

For some, the majestic Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is an official marker of the transition into the Christmas season in New York City.

Americans can watch the live telecast on both NBC and Peacock on Thursday, November 26, from 8:30 a.m. to noon in all time zones, while Telemundo will air a Spanish-language simulcast hosted by Andrea Meza, Aleyda Ortiz, and Clovis Nienow. For late risers, an encore will air starting at 2 p.m. ET/PT, and the full broadcast will also be on NBC with live audio description on Secondary Audio Program channel (SAP). Behind-the-scenes footage will be shared on social media @macys and #MacysParade via Instagram, TikTok, and Threads.

To rev up for the turkey day excitement, “Countdown to the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade” will air on Wednesday, November 25, on NBC and Peacock. The primetime special will broadcast live from the parade starting line with exclusive previews and behind-the-scenes stories from the balloons and floats.

One of the most underrated—and free—ways to experience the parade is by attending the Thanksgiving Eve balloon inflating event on Wednesday, November 25, a “time-honored tradition and special peek into the parade celebrations,” Coss says. Since 1994, the Macy’s Thanksgiving Parade has invited guests to see the process the balloons undergo to reach their larger-than-life size and scale the afternoon before Thanksgiving. Last year’s took place between 1 p.m. and 6 p.m., with the line opening at noon.

Those interested can enter at West 72nd Street and Columbus Avenue, where they’ll be guided through a security checkpoint and then can roam between West 77th and 81st Streets to view the balloons. Note that prohibited items include bags or backpacks larger than 12-by-6-by-12 inches, lawn chairs, large coolers, alcoholic beverages, chairs, weapons, drones, pets, and umbrellas; participants will be screened before entering the route.

For the latest up-to-date information, visit macys.com/parade for details on the parade and nbc.com/macys-thanksgiving-day-parade for updates on the broadcast.

#6212. Flights In Europe Face Endless Bomb Threats: “This Is Only The Beginning”

It has been a rather rough week for many airlines in Europe, as dozens of flights have been diverted, canceled, or delayed, due to bomb threats. There’s obviously some sort of a coordinated effort here, but it’s hard to know what exactly is going on, beyond just the desire to create chaos (thanks to 1990_ for flagging this)…

The concept of bomb threats being called in on flights is nothing new. Sometimes people are dumb enough to call in a bomb threat because they’re running late for a flight, and think that’s the best way not to miss it. Other times people will call in bomb threats as a prank.

Rarely is a bomb threat actually called in on a flight where there’s a bomb. That comes down to two reasons — it’s exceedingly rare for flights to be bombed (thank goodness), and if someone actually wants to take down a plane, they wouldn’t issue a warning, since that kind of defeats the purpose.

So that brings us to what has gone on in Europe this week, particularly on Tuesday, Thursday, and again today (Friday). Dozens of flights across airlines have had bomb threats called in on them, and airlines generally have to take these seriously. This has now happened to over 50 flights, departing from roughly a dozen countries.

In some cases the bomb threats were called in before takeoff, so passengers could be deplaned, allowing a search to happen before departure. In other cases, the threats came in mid-flight, leading to diversions, and even fighter jet escorts, in some situations.

In no case were any credible threats found, though. It goes without saying that this is incredibly frustrating for all parties. This is a massive waste of time and resources, given that these kinds of threats are consistently fake. At the same time, governments and airlines have to take these threats seriously, because imagine what would happen if a threat were proven to be real, and it was ignored (personally I think they should just be ignored, but that’s neither here nor there).

It’s not known for sure who is behind this attack, or just how centrally coordinated it is, rather than there being a copycat element to this.

Some emails taking credit for these attacks were signed as being from “the fighters of the Male State,” referencing a Russian far right, ultra nationalist movement that was founded in 2016. However, in a Telegram post today, the group’s founder denied involvement in this, and said the group hasn’t even existed since 2021.

Another email sent to media outlets regarding these attacks said that “this is only the beginning,” and threatened further attacks (or at least threats of attacks) across European transport.

The timing of this is likely not a coincidence, as Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky is currently visiting Europe for a series of meetings regarding the war with Russia.

It goes without saying that this could get messy. If this is really coming out of Russia, it’ll be hard for European authorities to hold them accountable. And it’s also easy enough for the culprits to try to mask where their threats come from.

If the threats keep coming, then one wonders how this will be handled — will this all just continue, or will the threats be ignored at some point?

Dozens of flights across Europe have been impacted by bomb threats this week, which is obviously incredibly frustrating. None were found to be credible, but they’ve all been taken seriously, with everything from aircraft evacuations, to diversions, to fighter jet escorts.

It can be hard to track down the source of these threats, especially if it’s some tech-savvy, foreign operation. An email claiming to be associated with the group behind these threats suggest that this is only the beginning. Only time will tell how this plays out, because if the threats continue and authorities have no way to take action against the foreign culprits, their options might be limited.

What do you make of this Europe airplane bomb threat situation?

#6211. Singapore Airlines’ New Business Class Finishes Look Cheap, Mismatched

Earlier I covered how Singapore Airlines unveiled its new first & business class, which should enter service in 2027 (hopefully). These products look like very nice improvements over the existing cabins, even if they’re not revolutionary.

That being said, I have to give Singapore Airlines some tough love on the new business class seats. Let me acknowledge that I’m a huge fan of Singapore Airlines as a brand. Any list I keep of the best airlines in the world (whether it’s the best airline brand, best first class, best business class, best inflight service, best inflight entertainment, etc.) has Singapore Airlines on it… that’s how highly I think of the brand!

But I’m also honest, regardless of how it fits my preconceived notions of a brand. I feel like I’m saying what everyone else is thinking, seemingly except for most influencers who are in Singapore for the launch event, who are just casually glossing over this… so much for attention to detail!

When I think of Singapore Airlines, the first thing that comes to mind for me is how deliberate the airline is. I don’t think there’s an airline that’s more intentional with every aspect of its guest experience, from the tone of voice with which staff speak, to warm and elegant design.

I’d say Singapore Airlines’ new first class actually looks really on brand. It’s a nice evolution of what the carrier has historically offered — it’s warm and elegant without being outdated.

And then you move to business class, and it looks like Scoot and Spirit Airlines had a baby. The gray and black is generic, the yellow accents look cheap, and then there’s so much going on with the blue and white bulkheads (if that’s actually how they’ll look).

And the Scoot reference isn’t even sarcastic. For those not familiar, Scoot is Singapore Airlines’ low cost carrier, and look at the seat finishes you’ll find there!

Usually there’s some consistency between seat finishes and wider branding, including the livery, flight attendant uniforms, etc. In this case, it’s not only not aligned, but they seem at odds with one another. There’s otherwise not a hint of yellow (or neon green, or whatever that is) in Singapore Airlines’ branding.

What so bizarre to me is how the first and business class finishes are completely mismatched, and you wouldn’t assume they belonged to the same airline. That’s because Singapore Airlines worked with different design firms (separate from the seating manufacturers as such) for the two cabins.

BMW Designworks was behind the business class seats, while PriestmanGoode was behind the first class seats. I think it’s safe to say there was no coordination between the two. I guess the argument from executives is that they want the cabin to look more modern and high tech, and go after a younger crowd, but I just don’t follow the logic.

It’s clear that Singapore Airlines put many years of effort into this product, and frankly I’m just surprised that Singapore Airlines executives signed off on this. Am I just in the minority in thinking this isn’t a good look for the airline? Did some marketer assure Singapore Airlines executives this was great branding, and they were wrong? Or did everyone just independently decide that this looks great?

If they at least eliminated the yellow stripes, it would no longer look cheap, but would instead look generic. I’m just surprised that this is the conclusion they came to.

Singapore Airlines of course had a big media event in Singapore to celebrate the launch of this product. I don’t attend media events, just as a general policy, because I don’t find them to be a great use of time. But I certainly do enjoy seeing the coverage from others.

What I find fascinating is the inherent bias that exists when someone is invited to something. For example, if you look at the comments on my post about the new cabins, the single thing most commented on by OMAAT community members is how bad the business class colors look.

If you watched the videos on social media about this, there’s oddly no commentary on that. Admittedly I haven’t seen all the coverage, but the worst coverage I’ve seen is someone saying they “don’t mind” the colors, and that it’s a “big departure” from the old look. Okay, that’s not exactly an endorsement.

I also haven’t found a single person who attended the event who said “I love the new colors,” which probably tells you everything you need to know. For that matter, it’s one thing if people acknowledged “I realize the colors might not look good in pictures, but in person, it’s a different story.” But I haven’t heard that either.

To me this gets at the rather complicated relationship between so many brands and influencer types. If you can say all the things you love about the product, shouldn’t you also feel totally comfortable criticizing the parts of the experience you don’t like, though?

While we’re on this topic, let me add one more point. Being able to sit in seats at media events like this is of course cool, but it really doesn’t actually give you an impression of what it’s like to fly in a product, and that’s why it’s not something I particularly value, as an experience.

Of course a big business class seat is comfortable when you sit in it for a minute, and you’re filming content. But the real test of a product is when you spend hours in the seat, when you recline the seat into a bed, when you try to move your laptop around while you’re being served a meal, etc.

I once had the opportunity to spend a night in an aircraft seat on the ground (I can’t really say more, since I signed an NDA, but it was to provide feedback to a seating manufacturer). To me that was fascinating, because it really gives you an understanding of what the experience is like. My feeling about the seat was very different after being in the seat for many hours vs. when I sat down.

Singapore Airlines has unveiled its new cabins, and there’s a lot to be excited about, as the hard products look very nice. However, Singapore Airlines’ new business class cabin finishes are a real mystery to me, because the yellow stripe looks cheap (I mean, it seems to be inspired by the carrier’s low cost subsidiary), and completely mismatched with first class.

The airline used different design firms for first class and business class. For an airline so focused on attention to detail and being very deliberate in terms of design, this strikes me as a misstep. Anyway, Singapore Airlines, I still love you and think you’re one of the best airlines in the world…

Where do you stand on Singapore Airlines’ new business class seat finishes? Does anyone love them?

#6210. The 6 Military Aircraft Manufacturers Still Building New Combat Aircraft For The US Armed Forces In 2026

The United States military is one of the biggest purchasers of new aircraft. It's by far the largest military in the world, and its contracts with major suppliers represent crucial business. Some companies rely almost entirely on US defense contracts, and while the aviation industry as a whole is generally unkind to smaller players, several companies compete against one another for contracts and also specialize in their own niches.

This includes transport and support aircraft, as well as combat aircraft. Military aviation is most closely associated with combat aircraft, which are specialized planes and helicopters designed to destroy enemy targets. This can take the form of air superiority fighters, bomber aircraft, and strike aircraft.

Multi-role aircraft that can perform combat roles are also involved. These types of aircraft are flown by the US Air Force and Navy, as well as the US Army and US Marine Corps. Currently, there are six companies actively producing combat aircraft for the US armed forces.

A subsidiary of Textron, Bell primarily produces military helicopters for the US. The company currently produces the UH-1Y Venom, one of the latest versions of the famed Huey rotorcraft family. The original UH-1 Iroquois/Huey entered service in 1959, while the UH-1Y Venom was introduced in 2008. Compared to prior Huey variants (of which there have been several), the UH-1Y features modernized technology and a longer cabin.

The Venom can also be equipped with rockets, machine guns, and an electronic warfare pod. In addition, Bell builds the AH-1Z Viper, yet another derivative of the Huey. Whereas the UH-1Y Venom is primarily a utility helicopter that can also serve in combat roles, the AH-1Z Viper is designed as an attack rotorcraft.

It incorporates features like added weaponry and a narrower profile, while also featuring a different fuselage design for its mission role. The AH-1Z entered service in 2010, and although it looks dramatically different from the UH-1Y, the two helicopters have about 85% parts commonality. Adding to the Huey derivatives, Bell is working on the MV-75 Cheyenne II, a tiltrotor aircraft positioned as the replacement for aging UH-60 Black Hawks.

It will feature two tilting rotors (similar to the V-22 Osprey), but it will be far more capable than a traditional helicopter. The MV-75 is primarily being designed as a troop transport, but it will also feature an optional cannon and missiles for greater defensive capability. It's currently projected that the Cheyenne II will be ready for service by 2031.

Boeing is a major US defense contractor, but two of its most prominent military aircraft programs are actually derivatives of McDonnell Douglas designs. The Boeing F-15EX Eagle II is an improved variant of the F-15 Eagle, one of the most successful air superiority fighters of all time, and only entered service in 2024.

Meanwhile, Boeing also produces the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet, and it's currently in the early stages of development on the F-47 sixth-generation fighter, which will replace the F-22 Raptor. In addition, Boeing is currently producing the AH-6, which is a light gunship based on the earlier MH-6 Little Bird.

Producing airliners, freighters, and airliner-derived business jets

Producing military planes, helicopters, missiles, and space systems

Providing aftermarket support to Boeing customers

Notably, Boeing has tested an uncrewed version of the AH-6, which proved its ability to operate fully autonomously. Meanwhile, the AH-64 Apache is Boeing's larger attack helicopter offering, originally developed by Hughes Helicopters and later built by McDonnell Douglas before the merger with Boeing. Currently, the Apache is being produced as the AH-64E.

Alongside the wide array of combat fighters and helicopters, Boeing offers a diverse selection of military aircraft serving other roles. For example, it currently offers two transport helicopters in its lineup (consisting of the H-47 Chinook and the MH-139 Grey Wolf), while also selling the KC-46 Pegasus aerial refueler. The manufacturer is actively delivering the P-8 Poseidon, and Boeing also produces the MQ-25 Stingray, a carrier-based drone capable of aerial refueling.

The United States produced around 150 fighter jets in 2024 and is expected to produce up to 250 in 2025, as well as other specialized jet aircraft.

General Atomics Aeronautical Systems is well known for its lineup of military drones. The company primarily focuses on uncrewed aerial vehicles and radar systems and currently produces the MQ-1C 25M Gray Eagle, as well as the MQ-9B SkyGuardian/SeaGuardian. The Gray Eagle is a derivative of the General Atomics MQ-1 Predator, which entered service in 1995 and has since been retired by the USAF, while the MQ-1C is designed specifically for the US Army.

The MQ-9 Reaper is a significantly larger, faster, and more capable UAV than the MQ-1, incorporating a turboprop engine, which allows for much greater payloads. In addition, the MQ-9 can be controlled by the same ground systems as the MQ-1. Currently, General Atomics is producing the aircraft as the MQ-9B SkyGuardian and SeaGuardian.

The SkyGuardian features advanced systems and performance improvements for operations in civilian airspace, whereas the SeaGuardian is designed for naval aviation. General Atomics is currently developing the MQ-20 Avenger, the next evolution of its UAV line.

Unlike its predecessors, the Avenger will be powered by a turbofan engine, while also incorporating stealth features. The UAV is designed to carry other uncrewed systems to achieve stand-off survivability and penetrating capability, and can still use the same ground systems as the MQ-1 and MQ-9 families.

Lockheed Martin is one of the most iconic aerospace manufacturers in history. The company is most famous for the SR-71 Blackbird, as well as aircraft like the C-130 Hercules, C-141 Starlifter, C-5 Galaxy, F-117 Nighthawk, and the relatively new F-22 Raptor. Today, Lockheed Martin produces two fighter jets, with its F-35 Lightning II quickly becoming the backbone of the US armed forces' fighter jet fleet.

The F-35 is the second-most common fighter used by the US, as well as the most common stealth fighter in the world. Lockheed Martin also currently produces the F-16V Viper. The F-16 was originally developed by General Dynamics in the 1970s, and Lockheed acquired the F-16 program in 1993 (it later merged with Martin Marietta to become Lockheed Martin in 1995).

The upgraded F-16V Viper debuted in 2021, and it features a new radar, updated avionics, more advanced cockpit screens, and electronic warfare suites. In addition to the two fighters currently in production, Lockheed Martin is actively developing 'Vectis', a new uncrewed combat drone.

Unlike prior UAVs like the MQ-9, Vectis will be AI-powered rather than being remotely piloted, and it's intended to serve as a 'loyal wingman' to assist crews piloting fifth-generation/sixth-generation fighters. It will be similar in size to a fighter jet and will feature a stealth design, while its weapons arsenal will make it a highly versatile tool once it enters service.

The world's most valuable aircraft manufacturing companies make commercial, private, and military aircraft including helicopters and eVTOL aircraft.

Northrop Grumman is famous for building a wide variety of aircraft, with the relatively recent B-2 Spirit flying wing bomber being one of the company's most successful designs. But the B-2 Spirit entered service in 1997, and its stealth technology is no longer cutting-edge, while production of the Spirit (which was produced in limited numbers) ended 26 years ago.

It's an expensive aircraft to fly and maintain, which is why the USAF awarded a contract to Northrop Grumman for a replacement. The Northrop Grumman B-21 Raider retains the same flying wing design as the B-2 Spirit, but it's smaller and lighter than its predecessor. It features more advanced stealth technology, and crucially, it will be cheaper to produce than the B-2 Spirit.

As the USAF plans to operate over 100 examples, the B-21 will be less expensive to acquire per unit, while maintenance costs will be lower as well. It will carry slightly less payload, but will be more survivable and feature a modular open systems architecture. In addition to the B-21 Raider, Northrop Grumman is currently producing the E-2 Hawkeye and developing the YFQ-48 Talon Blue.

Similar to the Lockheed Martin Vectis, this is an uncrewed combat aerial vehicle that will be powered by AI systems to assist pilots operating fighter jets. The first flight for this loyal wingman aircraft is currently projected for late 2026, and it will be one of multiple loyal wingman designs that will be an integral part of the USAF fleet.

Sikorsky Aircraft, currently owned by Lockheed Martin, has been mass-producing helicopters for over 80 years. It produces rotorcraft for the civilian and military markets, with the S-70 line being its primary model. The type is most prominently produced as the UH-60 Black Hawk, a utility/transport helicopter used extensively by the US military, but Sikorsky also manufactures combat variants of the S-70 line.

The MH-60 Sea Hawk is a variant for the US Navy, which is capable of performing anti-submarine warfare, anti-surface warfare, naval special warfare, search & rescue, combat search & rescue, vertical replenishment, and medevac roles. The HH-60 Pave Hawk, meanwhile, is primarily used by the USAF for special operations insertions and recoveries, as well as combat search & rescue.

#6209. 8 Dreamy Hotels Our NYC Editors Are Booking This Winter

If there’s one thing the editors at Condé Nast Traveler love, it’s weekendmaxxing. We’re all about scouting the very best hotels upstate, or catching a quick flight to Miami, all before returning back to our New York City office by Monday. The art of the weekend trip becomes especially important in the wintertime, when the city closes its blinds and hibernates until spring. This is when an off-season jaunt to the Rockaways, or a hideaway in a Berkshires lodge, becomes all the more appealing. Essentially, we love a trip where you can get cozy somewhere else—because sometimes all you need is a simple change of scenery to tackle the winter blues.

From wellness sanctuaries nestled in the Catskills to country retreats in New England, these are the hotels our editors are eyeing for when the weather turns brisk, all within a few hours of NYC or a short flight away.

Where are you staying? Mayflower Inn & Spa, Washington, Connecticut

What drew you to this hotel? I visited Mayflower Inn back in spring 2024 with one of my best friends while she was pregnant with her second baby, and I’ve been dying to go back ever since. I don’t know if I’ve ever felt more relaxed than I did while there—we spent hours in the spa, chatted by the firepits, stuffed ourselves with farm-fresh meals, and feasted our eyes on some incredible interior design.

What are you eating? I won’t be leaving the hotel for food, that’s for sure. I’m always impressed by the F&B at Auberge properties, and the Mayflower Inn was no exception. The Garden Room offers creative but approachable seasonal cuisine from breakfast through dinner (don’t skip the burger), and the Tap Room is where you’ll find a tavern-style food menu plus a mixologist slinging delicious cocktails and mocktails.

What do you hope to get up to in the area? The Mayflower Inn is located in Washington, Connecticut, a small town in Litchfield County, a region beloved by many of my colleagues. Next time I visit the hotel, I’ll have to make a few stops along the way to see what all the fuss is about.

Where are you staying? Urban Cowboy Lodge, Big Indian, New York

What drew you to this hotel? Urban Cowboy Lodge has been on my weekend getaway wish list for years, and there’s something about it in winter that feels particularly charming—maybe it’s the delightful snow-filled view from the bathtub (pictured above) that drew me in. I’m imagining myself curled up with a good book by the lounge’s fireplace, draped in a Pendleton blanket, then dipping into the aforementioned copper clawfoot bathtubs. At just about two-and-a-half hours north of Manhattan, it’s a not-too-far excursion I’m saving for when I really need a break from winter in the city.

What are you eating? Phoenicia Diner, of course. I’m also keen to try out some of the many craft beers at Ralph’s Bar.

What do you hope to get up to in the area? I’m not a skier, so in the winter, heading to the Catskills comes with more of a stay-indoors-and-get-cozy vibe for me. Besides a pit stop at Phoenicia Diner, I imagine the furthest I’ll trek is over to the sauna and bowling alley.

Where are you staying? The Rockaway Hotel & Spa, Rockaway Park, New York

What drew you to this hotel? Aside from the ocean views—poetically perfect for New York in the winter—The Rockaway is home to one of my favorite wellness scenes in the city. The space transforms its outdoor pool area (which, in the summer months, is home to outdoor concerts and DJ-led pool parties) into the cozy Winter Pool House. The space gets decked out with outdoor cedar barrel saunas and the softest plush robes to wear while you transition to the heated outdoor pool. The warm water mixed with the ice-cold breeze coming off the nearby coastline is glorious.

What are you eating? I’ll be heading to Margie’s—the mood-lit hotel lobby restaurant—and ordering a juicy cheeseburger and a frosty gin martini. What better way to warm your soul?

What do you hope to get up to in the area? The beauty of visiting this hotel in winter? No summer beach crowds. I’ll likely bundle up, head to the beach for some meditation, and head right back to my cozy room at The Rockaway to soak up the views even more.

Where are you staying? Wildflower Farms, Auberge Collection, Gardiner, New York

What drew you to this hotel? I’ve had Wildflower Farms on my wish list for the past few years. Every photo I see of the property on Instagram looks so dreamy. It feels like a true escape from the city—quiet, cozy, and restful. Located in New York’s Hudson Valley, it’s a quick 90-minute drive from NYC, making it a convenient pick for couples or families seeking an easy getaway.

What are you eating? I’m most eager to have coffee and pastries around the fire at the Great Porch, Wildflower’s open-air communal space with sprawling views of the Shawangunk Ridge. And of course, I’ll be dining at the resort’s on-site restaurant, Clay, where the rustic American menu is full of seasonal ingredients from local farms.

What do you hope to get up to in the area? I usually try to pack as many activities and must-try coffee shops and restaurants as possible into my trip itinerary, but Wildflower Farms encourages you to slow down. You’ll find me at Thistle, the resort’s on-site spa where hand-harvested, small-batch oils and scrubs are used during tailored treatments.

Where are you staying? Inness, Accord, New York

What drew you to this hotel? Inness is resplendent in the summer, so I’ve always been keen to see a different side of it come hunker-down weather. Its cabins are certainly primed for rest, thanks to the fireplaces, but there’s also the outdoor pit with prime-time views of the Catskill Mountains decked in snow. I also love the central farmhouse, where cozy seats call out for a great book and a hot cocoa. And if you can drag yourself out, which you should, there are loads of hikes and walks, including those along the Ashokan Reservoir, which is one of my favorite spots.

What are you eating? Stacks of pancakes; comfort-food entrées like risottos; a round of Dorato Negronis at the bar.

What do you hope to get up to in the area? Spending the afternoons shopping and dining in some of my favorite nearby towns, like Kingston and Woodstock.

Where are you staying? Four Seasons Hotel at The Surf Club, Surfside, Florida

What drew you to this hotel? When one of my best friends announced she was celebrating her 30th birthday in Miami, a city I’ve shockingly never been to, the first place I thought of was the Four Seasons Hotel at the Surf Club; I remember reading about its incredible celebrity guest history, which includes everyone from Frank Sinatra to Elizabeth Taylor.

What are you eating? Perhaps we’d start with a toast at the on-site Champagne Bar, then move on over to dinner at Lido for seafood-inspired pastas.

What do you hope to get up to in the area? Laze around by the pool, enjoy the quieter beaches of Surfside, and maybe stroll through the Rubell Museum in Allapattah.

Where are you staying? Tourists, North Adams, Massachusetts

What drew you to this hotel? I love heading north of the city in the colder months—leaning in and getting even colder and cozier. And the words “reimagined motor lodge” are another form of catnip for me. I love the sense of nostalgia paired with very plush, updated interiors, ideal for hiding out for a wintery weekend.

What are you eating? I’d carve out time for the hotel’s restaurant, the Airport Room, ideally timed to one of the chef pop-ups they do—though given the three-and-a-half-hour drive from New York City, I’d probably also plot out an en route lunch in Kingston as well.

What do you hope to get up to in the area? Wintery hikes on the nearby trails, lots of reading by the fireplace, and maybe some of the arts and crafts activities—why not.

Where are you staying? Eastwind, Windham, New York

What drew you to this hotel? When I first caught sight of Eastwind, I was really into the property’s sprawl—there are different types of accommodations (cabins, hotel-style rooms), and everything is wound together via a small trail system lined with fairy lights, from the beer garden to the main house. It feels like a really great spot to get away from the noise of New York City.

What are you eating? The on-site restaurant, Dandie’s, serves up barbecue in a cozy, window-lined space—get some house-made gelato for dessert. And definitely make a detour for brunch at Phoenicia Diner on your way back to the city.

What do you hope to get up to in the area? Stop by Harriman State Park for a hike to stretch your legs on the way north. Once you’re there, you’ve got skiing options (Windham Mountain Club), more hiking trails (The Windham Path), and indoor activities (Helsinki Hudson for music lovers; Olana Historic Estate for museum enthusiasts).

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6208. When Is An Airport Lounge Visit Not Worth It? Here’s How I Decide…

It goes without saying that a lot about the passenger experience when traveling by air has changed over the decades, both for better and worse. I think perhaps one of the most fascinating transformations we’ve seen over the years involves airport lounges, and how their purpose has completely flipped.

I’d like to talk about that in a bit more detail in this post, and share my approach to using lounges. Let me emphasize that there are of course all kinds of lounges out there, from international first class lounges, to international business class lounges, to Priority Pass, membership, and credit card lounges. This post is primarily about lounges that fall into that last category, in terms of being pretty widely accessible.

Look, I’m not trying to sound like some boomer talking about how things were in “the good old days” (nothing against boomers… hi, dad!), but I think it’s interesting to compare how things were 15-20 years ago, to how they are today.

Back in the day, airport lounges — even the most basic ones — were primarily about escaping the hustle and bustle of the terminal, and having a quiet place from which to work, with free Wi-Fi and easy access to charging ports. At the time, free Wi-Fi and charging ports in terminals were incredibly rare. The food in most standard domestic lounges sucked — it was typically cubed cheese, snack mix, and not a whole lot else.

It also goes without saying that lounges were mostly very poorly monetized. Airport real estate is incredibly expensive, and lounges were primarily a cost center for their operators, as part of an overall value proposition for travelers.

Fast forward to today, and look at the state of lounges in the United States. Lounges have much better food than they used to, and they also have much better amenities than they used to. Also, exponentially more people have access to the lounges than they used to. They’re actually pretty nice destinations in airports.

The catch is that they’ve completely lost their initial purpose — they’re no longer a place you go to escape the crowds, and quite to the contrary, they’re often the most crowded place in a terminal. In many lounges you’ll find every single seat occupied, and even a very long waitlist to get in.

Obviously this is great for monetization, since lounge operators maximize their return by having the lounges utilized as much as possible, so that the cost can be divided by the highest number of people possible. Ironically, we’ve also seen terminals largely get much nicer over the years. It’s nowadays common to see free Wi-Fi and charging ports throughout terminals, and it’s usually not too hard to just find a quiet place to sit, with more peace than you’d find in a lounge.

Back in the day, if I had lounge access, my obvious move was always to use the lounge if I had time. I mean, that seems like a pretty obvious move, right? After all, you get access to something “premium,” so you want to make the most of it. Most people with TSA PreCheck don’t say “meh, you know, I think I’ll skip that today and go through the regular line.”

At the same time, I think one has to step back and look at things objectively. At times it almost feels like people use lounges religiously in order to justify the annual fees on their credit cards, and so they can talk about how they’re eating for “free.”

You’ll often see people on social media essentially call airport lounges upper middle class airport cafeterias, and that’s probably not actually too far off in terms of how they’re practically used… and there’s nothing wrong with that!

Personally, for places with consistently crowded lounges, my approach to lounge use is pretty straightforward:

Honestly, this is one of the reasons I really love grab & go lounges, where you can pick up something to take with you. To me that’s the ideal setup, since it serves the purpose I’m actually looking for from lounges — if a lounge is going to be crowded, I’d rather just be able to grab what I’d like, and head somewhere quiet.

As someone who loves coffee, it’s why I also appreciate when lounges have great coffee to go. It’s typically the item I most want to consume at airports, and the wait for a cup of coffee at an airport can often be quite long early in the morning.

The lounge crowding issue nowadays is only made worse by the number of people who are watching videos and making calls with no headphones in lounges.

The whole concept of airport lounges has changed massively over the years. Monetization of lounges has largely gotten better, as they’ve become a key component of the credit card race that we’re seeing between airlines and card issuers.

That’s a double edged sword. On the one hand, lounges have become higher quality, on average. On the other hand, demand for them has also increased massively.

For the most part, lounges are no longer a place you go to escape the bustle of the terminal, and to use free Wi-Fi and charge your electronics. Now they’re a place you go to eat, drink, and wait in line.

The way I’ve used lounges has definitely evolved over the years, and it’s one of the reasons I appreciate the grab & go concept that we’re increasingly seeing. Unless I’m hungry or thirsty, I prefer just finding a quiet gate area.

What do you make of how airport lounges have evolved, and has your approach to using them changed?

#6207. 11 US Vacation Rentals Where the Hot Tub Comes With a View

Travelers love to debate window vs. aisle, or whether or not a group trip is a good idea, but I’ve never met anyone who didn’t love a hot tub. It’s the amenity that separates a good vacation home from a great one—the ultimate way to wake up your system in the morning or relax tired muscles in the evening, no matter the season. The rentals on this list, from cozy log cabins in Tennessee to glassy beach houses in coastal Oregon, all promise steamy hot tubs worth planning a trip around. Whether you want to experience the stillness of the New Mexican desert, breathe in the Blue Ridge mountain air, or look out for wildlife in Texas Hill Country, you can do it all from the comfort of your very own bubbling sanctuary. For a rejuvenating weekend away, where the agenda is resetting your nervous system or simply sharing a few laughs with friends, these hot tub–included rentals in the US are just the ticket.

We've selected these listings based on Superhost status, ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews.

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: In-unit washer/dryer, game room, outdoor space

Just a short drive away from some of Tennessee’s best theme parks (including Dollywood), this Smoky Mountain retreat is a home the entire family will love. The 2,100-square-foot cabin is divided into three levels, each with its own bedroom (all have king-size beds) and bathroom (one has a freestanding bathtub). Kids will love the game room in the loft, as well as a few hours spent at nearby Wild Bear Falls Indoor Water Park, Anakeesta, or Ripley's Aquarium of the Smokies. After all that fun, adults can end their days in the outdoor hot tub, perfectly positioned for watching the sun set over the mountain ridge.

Location: Gatlinburg, TennesseeThings to do nearby: Historic Ogle Log Cabin, Hillbilly Golf, Herbert Holt Park

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Pet-friendly, floor-to-ceiling windows, forest views

Ideal for a couples getaway in the woods, this glassy cabin, with its soaring, floor-to-ceiling windows, is sure to provide a nature-friendly reset. It’s located just a five-minute walk away from Hocking Hills State Park and has all the modern comforts you need: a newly renovated kitchen and dining area, a queen-size bed upstairs, and, of course, an outdoor patio with a firepit and hot tub for nights spent nestled in the trees. Many reviewers gush over how spotless the place is and how close it is to hiking trails. One thing to note: AWD/4WD vehicles are recommended due to the rugged landscape.

Location: Laurelville, OhioThings to do nearby: Hocking Hills State Park, Conkles Hollow State Nature Preserve, Cedar Falls

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 3.5 bathsWhy we love it: Game room, home gym, lake views

This modern masterpiece of a home, perfect for large family gatherings, was voted a 2026 Vrbo Vacation Rental of the Year. And it’s pretty easy to understand why, between the gorgeous views of Squam Lake from nearly every corner; the private dock from which to swim, kayak, or paddleboard; and the hot tub that’s built into the property. There are dozens of hiking trails nearby, whether you want to go on an easy lakeside stroll or trek to Mount Morgan. Suitable for any season, the house invites you to either laze a sunny day away on the patio’s sun chairs or curl up by the fireplace on a cooler night.

Location: Center Harbor, New HampshireThings to do nearby: Lake Winnipesaukee, White Mountain National Forest, Loon Mountain Resort

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Cold plunge, meditation spaces, outdoor shower

For a Hudson Valley hideaway just minutes from Catskill State Park, this two-bedroom home is bound to bring you peace, with reading nooks, meditation spaces, and even a room for massages, which you can book alongside a sound bath. There’s plenty to do outside too, whether that looks like meandering along the nearby Mill Stream, stretching out on the “flying saucer” hammock, or engaging in a little hydrotherapy (there’s a cedar cold plunge and hot tub situated right next to each other). In the warmer months, roast some s’mores by the firepit, and in the winter months, read a book by the wood-burning stove.

Beyond the expansive living room and fully equipped kitchen, there’s a bedroom downstairs with a queen-size bed, plus another one upstairs with a king-size bed and private balcony. When night falls, take in the stars from the hot tub on the outdoor patio and keep an eye out for local wildlife, which can include deer, turkeys, birds, and the occasional fox. Enjoy the local shops and breweries of nearby Wimberley Square, or go swimming or hiking at Jacob’s Well and Blue Hole Regional Park.

Experience the beauty of the Yucca Valley desert from this spacious one-bedroom home. Enjoy sunrise or sunset views from the outdoor stock tank pool or hot tub, and be sure to look out for animals. Previous guests have recorded a few sightings, from lizards and rabbits to coyotes and roadrunners.

Located just north of Manzanita in Tillamook County, this massive, five-bedroom home offers spectacular views of Neahkahnie Beach. Suitable for a family reunion or bachelorette weekend, it can sleep up to 12 guests and has large spaces built for gathering, whether that’s the grand dining table near the kitchen or the patio outside that includes the gorgeous hot tub. There’s plenty to do nearby, from strolling down Manzanita’s Laneda Avenue in search of a quaint coffee shop to visiting the historic Nehalem Bay Winery for a tasting.

At this El Prado property, you’ll have to make the tough call between hopping in the Japanese-style bathtub, the outdoor hot tub, or nearby Manby Hot Springs—but who says you can’t do all three? Located on 15 acres of land where juniper, piñon, and sage grow wild, the architectural home features cast-earth walls, a corrugated metal roof, radiant heat, and mahogany woodwork. Explore the many trails at Rio Grande Gorge National Monument, a minute’s walk away, then have a soak under the stars.

Whether you want to play pool in the game room, take in views of the forest from the hot tub, or explore nearby Grandfather Mountain State Park, there’s no shortage of ways to spend your days. The fully equipped kitchen has everything you need to prepare meals at home, while the patio has a barbecue for outdoor entertaining. The wood-burning fireplace and blanket ladder in the living room make movie nights especially cozy.

While there are only three bedrooms, the home can actually sleep up to 10, thanks to the help of bunk beds and sleeper sofas. It’s time to take that ski trip out of the group chat.

Planning and taking a trip can be exciting, but unexpected events can disrupt even the most meticulously organized vacations. Sudden illness, severe weather and unforeseen circumstances can throw a wrench in the works, forcing you to change your plans and seek compensation.

Fortunately, many credit cards include trip cancellation and interruption insurance at no additional cost when you use your card to book travel. The right card can reimburse nonrefundable expenses if your plans fall apart.

Here are the best credit cards for trip cancellation and interruption insurance — and how their coverage compares.

*Eligibility and benefit level varies by card. Terms, conditions and limitations apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company.

The cards listed above offer some of the strongest trip cancellation and interruption protections available. However, many other travel credit cards also include some form of coverage — often with lower limits.

Related: Credit cards with travel insurance

Trip cancellation and trip interruption insurance can reimburse prepaid, nonrefundable travel expenses if you cancel or alter your trip for a covered reason. Coverage limits, eligible expenses and qualifying events vary by card.

In general, trip cancellation insurance applies when you must cancel before departure, and trip interruption insurance applies if your trip is cut short after it begins.

Unlike travel insurance policies with optional “cancel for any reason” coverage, credit card coverage typically applies only to specific covered events outlined in your card’s guide to benefits. Covered reasons often include illness, injury or severe weather, but exclusions apply.

Because benefits can change, always review your card’s guide before booking travel.

Related: Should you get travel insurance if you have credit card protection?

Chase credit cards offer some of the most comprehensive trip cancellation and interruption protections among major issuers.

The and the each provide coverage of up to $10,000 per covered person and $20,000 per trip. Despite their different annual fees, $95 and $795, respectively, both cards offer top-tier protection limits.

The , United's highest-tier personal card and the one best suited for frequent United travelers, also provides coverage of up to $10,000 per covered person and $20,000 per trip, per the card's Guide to Benefits.

You and your immediate family members may be eligible for coverage when you pay for all or a portion of your trip with an eligible Chase card or redeem rewards associated with that account, including through Chase Travel℠.

Other Chase cards offer lower limits. For example, the (see rates and fees), the (see rates and fees) and the (see rates and fees) typically provide coverage of up to $5,000 per covered person and $10,000 per trip.

Meanwhile, cards such as the (see rates and fees), the (see rates and fees) and the (see rates and fees) also offer trip cancellation and interruption insurance but with lower coverage limits. These cards typically reimburse only nonrefundable common carrier fares and offer significantly smaller per-person caps than the Sapphire cards.

Coverage generally applies only to the portion of the trip charged to your eligible card (or booked using associated rewards).

For example, if you pay for a nonrefundable hotel stay with gift cards but charge your flight to your Chase card, you likely won’t be reimbursed for the hotel if you cancel — even if the flight was covered.

Always consult your card’s guide to benefits for full terms, conditions and exclusions.

Related: Your guide to Chase’s trip insurance coverage

Select American Express cards offer trip cancellation and trip interruption insurance. Each benefit provides coverage of up to $10,000 per covered trip, with a separate maximum of $20,000 per eligible card per 12 consecutive months.

*Eligibility and benefit level varies by card. Terms, conditions and limitations apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company.

Unlike many issuers, eligible American Express cards may also cover traveling companions, not just immediate family members. A traveling companion is defined as someone who has made advance arrangements to travel with you or your family members for all or part of a covered trip.

To qualify, you must charge the full cost of round-trip common carrier transportation to an eligible Amex card or use a combination of your card and Membership Rewards points, vouchers or loyalty program certificates.

You can find benefit guides for eligible cards on Amex’s website.

Related: Your complete guide to travel protections on American Express cards

Who is covered by credit card trip cancellation and interruption insurance varies greatly. For example, eligible premium Chase cards cover the cardholder and immediate family members when the cardholder pays for all or a portion of a trip with their card account or rewards associated with their account.

On the other hand, eligible American Express cards cover the cardholder, their family members and traveling companions. The guide to benefits for eligible Amex cards defines a traveling companion as “an individual who has made advanced arrangements with you or your Family Members to travel together for all or part of a Covered Trip.”

Definitions of “family member” and “traveling companion” differ, and benefits are subject to change. Review your guide to benefits to confirm eligibility before booking.

Related: Are authorized users covered by Chase’s credit card travel insurance?

A benefits administrator can usually walk you through specific steps to make your claim. Luckily, many card issuers also allow you to make claims online, so you may not even need to hop on the phone to send any physical documents.

Related: Who is covered by credit card travel insurance?

Generally, trip cancellation and trip interruption insurance will cover nonrefundable expenses if you need to cancel your trip (or the remainder of your trip) due to a natural disaster. However, credit card insurance policies vary, so check your benefits guide for specific exclusions.

Note that you must book your trip before the natural disaster starts to be covered. If a storm or hurricane is named and you book your trip afterward, you likely won’t be covered.

Related: 4 times your credit card’s travel insurance can help with travel woes, and 7 times it won’t

Trip cancellation and interruption insurance can be one of the most valuable — and overlooked — benefits on a travel credit card.

Coverage details vary widely by issuer and by card, so it’s important to review your guide to benefits before booking.

For expensive trips, you may still consider stand-alone travel insurance, but the right credit card can provide meaningful protection without paying extra.

Related: Flight canceled or delayed? Here’s what to do next

#6205. How To Combine Marriott Bonvoy Points Between Accounts For Free

The major hotel loyalty programs all have different policies when it comes to combining points between accounts belonging to different members.

For example, Hilton Honors lets you transfer points to any other member online, and you can transfer up to 500,000 points and receive up to two million points per account per calendar year. Meanwhile World of Hyatt lets you transfer points to any other member online as well, with the ability to give or receive up to 525,000 points per year.

Marriott Bonvoy is the world’s largest loyalty program, so how does the program’s policy on combining points compare? Not very favorably, but it can still prove to be quite useful. I’d like to go over the details of how this feature of the program works.

Marriott Bonvoy lets you combine points between accounts at no cost, with the following restrictions:

There’s no need to be related to the person you’re sharing points with, or even to share the same address. Rather you can transfer your points to any member.

The only limitation is how long accounts have to be active:

Qualifying activity includes any earning or redeeming of points, with the exception of gifting or transferring points, receiving points as a gift or transfer, or earning points through social media programs.

Along those lines, it’s also worth pointing out that combining points with a member won’t count toward extending the expiration of your points, if that’s something you’re going for (Bonvoy points expire after 24 months of inactivity).

It’s possible to combine Marriott Bonvoy points between accounts either by phone or via an online tool, so let’s go over both of those options.

It’s possible to transfer points to another Marriott Bonvoy member at this link. The member looking to transfer their points (rather than the recipient) should log into their account at that link, and they’ll then be brought to the points transfer tool.

On that page you’ll have to enter the recipient’s first and last name, Marriott Bonvoy number, and how many points you want to transfer (between 1,000 and 100,000).

You’ll then be asked to receive a verification code, either by email or text.

You’ll then receive confirmation that your request has been made. While the transfer tool suggests that it could take up to one hour for points to post, in reality they typically post instantly.

If for whatever reason you don’t want to use the online tool to transfer points to another Marriott Bonvoy member, you can continue to do this by phone. Here’s how the process works:

Now that we’ve established that you can transfer points, perhaps the bigger question is why you would want to. There are some circumstances where combining points between Marriott Bonvoy accounts could make a lot of sense:

Ford transfers 100,000 Bonvoy points to me every year. Why? Because he has a sizable Bonvoy points balance, I have the higher status with Marriott, and we usually travel together. There’s more value in having Bonvoy points in my account rather than his, so that we can take advantage of elite perks when redeeming points.

While Marriott Bonvoy isn’t the most generous when it comes to letting members combine points between accounts, this is still a functionality worth being aware of. There are plenty of circumstances where it could make sense to combine points, whether you’re looking to maximize elite benefits or book travel for others.

The major catch is the restriction on how old the accounts have to be, plus the limit on how many points you can transfer, and how often you can transfer points.

#6204. Delta Launches 7 New International Routes This Winter: See Full List Now

With the IATA Winter Season from late October to late March now in full swing, Delta Air Lines is making a wide range of interesting route additions throughout its route network. Between now and Sunday, March 28, 2027, when the IATA Summer Season starts, the Atlanta-based US 'big three' legacy carrier and SkyTeam founding member will launch seven new routes, excluding its short-term CES additions.

All of these corridors serve international destinations, and they are spread across six of the carrier's US hubs, according to schedule data from Cirium, an aviation analytics company. Some are short-haul while others serve long-haul destinations, but, in one way or another, they will all play an important role in Delta's forthcoming growth. Let's take a closer look at where and when they are launching.

November will see one addition for Delta: the transborder link between Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) and Vancouver International Airport (YVR) in the Canadian province of British Columbia. As of November 21, the carrier is set to serve this short-haul international route on a twice-daily basis, using Airbus A319s from its mainline fleet.

Delta has served this route on and off over the last two decades, with regional Delta Connection flights operating in 2007 and 2008. These services then returned from 2015 to 2018, during which time 2017 was the only year that Delta also flew mainline jets from Los Angeles to Vancouver. The West Coast hub has since become one of its most crucial bases, according to the carrier.

"Delta is the only carrier at LAX serving all of the airport’s top 10 markets with multiple daily flights, giving customers greater choice and flexibility across the destinations they travel to most."

Moving into December, three more new routes will join Delta's network. The longest is the corridor from Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) to Ben Gurion Airport (TLV) in Tel Aviv, Israel. These flights are set to operate three times a week as of December 19, 2026, with the A350 being Delta's aircraft of choice. It previously served this route from 2006 to 2011 and in 2023.

Closer to home, Delta will also launch flights on December 19, from John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) to Daniel Oduber Quirós International Airport (LIR) in Liberia, Costa Rica. In this instance, the carrier is set to use the A321neo, with these flights only running seasonally until May 2027. It previously served this route in 2008 and from 2013 to 2017 with mainline flights.

The third and final Delta route launch on December 19 of this year links its hub at Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW) with Queen Beatrix International Airport (AUA) in Oranjestad, Aruba. These weekly flights will also run seasonally until May of next year, with coverage split between the A321neo and the Boeing 737-900ER. Unlike the others, the carrier has never served this route before.

Delta unveils its biggest Delta One overhaul in years, featuring luxury dining, enhanced comfort and global expansion in 2027.

Delta's winter additions keep coming right until the end of the season, with three more routes being added on March 27, the last day before the IATA Summer Season. These are all long-haul corridors, with the new route from Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) to Tokyo Narita Airport (NRT) in Japan clearly implemented to fight back against growing competition from Alaska Airlines in the Northwest.

These flights will operate daily using the A330-900neo. Another daily addition with this aircraft type will be the new route from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport (AUS) in Texas to Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG) in France. Elsewhere, March 27 is also currently set to be the launch date for Delta's thrice-weekly Atlanta-Riyadh (RUH) flights. However, these have sold poorly and have been delayed.
