#6179. Southwest 737 Flew 44 Times Before Wind Damage Was Found

A Southwest Boeing 737 MAX 8 flew 44 times before maintenance crews discovered tail damage that investigators traced to a thunderstorm more than a week earlier. In a final report released Thursday, the National Transportation Safety Board said the damage went undetected through a scheduled maintenance check and caused a standby rudder control unit to operate abnormally.

The damage came to light after Southwest flight 746 experienced unexpected rudder movements on May 25, 2024, while flying from Phoenix to Oakland, California. All 175 passengers and six crew members were uninjured. The aircraft, registered N8825Q, sustained substantial damage.

The NTSB traced the damage to the night of May 16, when the jet was parked in New Orleans, and thunderstorms brought gusts of up to 73 knots, or about 84 mph. Investigators said the wind likely moved the rudder enough to damage ribs inside the vertical stabilizer where the standby rudder control unit was mounted.

At the time, Boeing’s 737 maintenance manual called for a special inspection after an extreme wind event but gave no wind speed at which the check was required. The manual listed signs such as an aircraft moving over its wheel chocks or leaving tire skid marks.

Southwest also lacked a process to notify maintenance control when a parked aircraft had been exposed to extreme winds. The jet flew the next morning without the inspection.

Over the next week, the aircraft completed 38 flights with no reported rudder or yaw damper problems. It then underwent scheduled maintenance in Houston on May 23, including a test of the standby hydraulic system. The procedure required a mechanic at the tail to verify that the rudder moved in response to pedal inputs.

Hangar video showed the rudder moving to the right but failing to move to the left. Investigators said no one was at the tail to verify the movement. Southwest’s maintenance records showed the test was signed off as passed, and the aircraft returned to service. The NTSB could not determine whether the test worsened the existing damage.

On the fourth flight the next day, a crew disconnected the yaw damper after reporting that it was overcorrecting in turbulence. The yaw damper uses the rudder to counter side-to-side motion.

The jet flew one more leg with the system listed as inoperative. It then passed a functional test, and the yaw damper was returned to service before Flight 746.

On the Oakland flight, the captain noticed momentary stiffness in the rudder pedals while turning onto the runway. Shortly after reaching 34,000 feet, he felt what he described as “a small amount of Dutch roll.” Both pilots felt the pedals move, and the oscillations recurred after the crew descended to 32,000 feet.

Flight data showed one episode of rudder and pedal oscillations lasting about 20 seconds, with no significant change in heading or bank angle. Investigators found that the abnormal movement appeared in the data from the first flight after the Houston maintenance check, before crews reported it. They observed it only when the yaw damper was engaged.

Southwest removed the aircraft from service after it landed in Oakland. The airline later inspected the rudder control unit mounting areas across its 737 MAX fleet and found no similar damage. It also added individual mechanic sign-offs to the hydraulic test and set up a process to alert maintenance control after extreme winds. Boeing revised its maintenance manual to require the special inspection at a wind threshold of 65 knots, or 75 mph.

#6178. The Airlines That Offer Amenity Kits To Economy Class Passengers In 2026

For decades, amenity kits were seen as a small but thoughtful touch that helped define the long-haul flying experience, with eye masks, socks, toothbrushes, and even branded pouches making their way into the hands of passengers across multiple cabins. While premium cabins have continued to refine and elevate their offerings, the story in economy class has been very different.

In 2026, complimentary amenity kits in economy are increasingly rare, largely confined to ultra-long-haul routes or a small group of full-service carriers seeking to differentiate their product. Rising costs, changing passenger expectations, and a stronger focus on unbundled fares have all contributed to the decline of the amenity kit in economy class. Many airlines now provide basic comfort items only on request.

Meanwhile, others have removed them entirely in favor of buy-on-board options or sustainability-driven reductions in single-use products. However, a handful of carriers still see value in offering amenity kits at the back of the plane, using them as a subtle branding tool and a way to enhance the long-haul experience.

Etihad Airways is one of the few full-service carriers that still hands out amenity kits in economy class, but only on long-haul flights exceeding roughly six hours. Rather than a disposable bag of single-use plastics, Etihad Airways' economy class amenity kit comes in the form of a reusable tote bag containing typical essentials.

These include noise-canceling earplugs, an eye shade, and a small hand cream, all presented more as comfort tools than luxury gifts. The focus, true to the carrier’s evolving inflight product strategy, leans into practicality and sustainability rather than high-end cosmetics. This approach from the carrier, based at Abu Dhabi International Airport (AUH), reflects a broader trend across the industry.

Specifically, when airlines still offer economy kits, they are often pared back and designed to be useful beyond the flight itself, with recyclable or recycled materials and minimal environmental impact. Aside from the amenity kits, Etihad Airways’ economy class provides a practical and comfortable travel experience.

It has seats that feature adjustable headrests and recline, allowing passengers to rest or work during their flights. Each seat is equipped with a personal entertainment screen that offers a wide selection of movies, TV programs, music, and games, ensuring passengers have access to in-flight entertainment throughout their journey.

Discover the unexpected comfort hiding in these long-haul economy seats.

Qantas has also bucked the trend by continuing to offer economy class amenity kits on selected long-haul international routes. According to the oneworld carrier's own inflight experience pages, these kits typically include a dental set, an eye mask, and earplugs, packaged in a decorative felt pouch made from recycled PET bottles.

This provides a strong example of how carriers are trying to balance comfort with environmental responsibility. Unlike in premium cabins, where high-end branded items are now common, Qantas’ economy class amenity kits aim for simple comfort and sustainability. However, only select long-haul and ultra-long-haul flights see these amenity kits in economy class.

A prime example is the carrier's non-stop service between Perth Airport (PER) and London Heathrow Airport (LHR). These flights, operated by the Boeing 787-9, can reach up to 17 hours in length. As such, any additional comforts like a complimentary amenity kit are sure to be appreciated by passengers.

On flights where the amenity kit is not offered as standard in economy class, Qantas offers a selection of additional travel essentials on request across its international network. Qantas is in the midst of one of its most ambitious fleet renewal programs in decades, transforming ultra-long-haul flying. A key part of this strategy is the introduction of next-generation Airbus aircraft.

These include the Airbus A350-1000ULR, which will be the key player in the carrier's non-stop Project Sunrise flights connecting Australia with Europe and the US. In total, the airline has committed to a massive order of over 200 new aircraft for the Qantas Group, with major types including the Airbus A220-300, Airbus A321XLR, Airbus A350-1000ULR, and Boeing 787 models among its future lineup.

The Airbus A220-300 is already in service with QantasLink, replacing older regional aircraft and offering passengers a lighter, quieter cabin with more space and modern amenities. Meanwhile, the A321XLR has started flying domestically and will soon operate longer-range international routes.

Emirates is well known around the world for its high level of luxury across all travel classes. The carrier, based at Dubai International Airport (DXB), still provides amenity kits in economy class, albeit primarily on long-haul services and often only on overnight flights.

Emirates' current range of amenity kits is particularly distinctive, designed in partnership with wildlife conservation groups and printed with hand-drawn artwork highlighting endangered species. These amenity kits typically include comfort basics like socks, an eye shade, earplugs, and a dental kit, all contained in a reusable pouch made from sustainable materials such as recycled polyester and paper.

Emirates' hard product is unrivaled, too. The carrier continues to reinforce its reputation as one of the world’s most dynamic long-haul airlines in 2026, blending fleet modernization with an industry-leading passenger experience.

The airline’s ambitious multi-billion-dollar retrofit program is now underway, with over 200 Airbus A380 and Boeing 777-300ER aircraft scheduled to receive refreshed cabins. These will feature next-generation seat designs across all classes, upgraded in-flight entertainment, and ultra-fast WiFi.

Qatar Airways has long had a reputation for exceptional service in all travel classes, and amenity kits in economy class are a key part of that effort, especially on ultra-long-haul flights. Earlier versions of Qatar Airways' amenity kits included essentials such as a lip balm from Institut Karité Paris, a Miradent dental kit, an eye mask, socks, and earplugs.

The airline even won industry accolades for the quality of its economy class offering in the past. However, in 2026, the situation is not quite as clear, with passenger reports indicating that amenity kits in Qatar Airways' economy class are not guaranteed on every flight.

They now tend to be distributed on select long overnight segments only, meaning that on shorter or daytime sectors, they may be absent entirely. Meanwhile, the oneworld carrier's premium cabins continue to draw attention for their luxury-branded amenity kits, underscoring the widening gap between premium cabin and economy class perks.

Across the industry, the days of universally handed-out amenity kits in economy class are largely behind us, with a combination of financial, environmental, and operational factors having driven this shift. Mounting cost pressures and the continued rise of unbundled fare models have encouraged airlines to strip back inclusions that many passengers now bring themselves.

These include toothbrushes and eye masks. At the same time, sustainability commitments are prompting carriers to reduce single-use plastics and eliminate items that frequently go unused, making large-scale distribution of amenity kits harder to justify.

Operational considerations also play a role, and even when economy amenity kits are still offered, they are typically reserved for ultra-long-haul or overnight services, where passenger comfort needs are greatest, and rest is a priority. As a result, availability can vary significantly by route and departure time.

Who do you think offers the better amenity kits?

In 2026, the most luxurious airline amenity kits are found not in economy but in premium cabins like first class and business class, as carriers compete to elevate their long-haul experience with high-end brands, exclusive collaborations, and truly indulgent products. These kits are less about simple comfort and more about delivering a sense of luxury that aligns with an airline’s overall premium service.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, given their reputation for exemplary onboard service, some of the standout premium airline amenity kits available today include those offered by Emirates, Qatar Airways, and Singapore Airlines. Emirates consistently tops the conversation for its ultra-luxurious kits, particularly in first class and business class.

The airline has partnered with Italian luxury brand Bvlgari to create kits that include exclusive fragrances, premium toiletries, and even gold-lacquered mirrors, wrapped in collectable faux-leather pouches. These touches reinforce the carrier's reputation for opulence in the skies.

Qatar Airways is another airline to offer an industry-leading amenity kit, especially since partnering with French perfumer Diptyque. These elegant kits often contain scented body care, face creams, and eau de toilette, all presented in a stylish pouch that enhances the premium experience.

Meanwhile, Singapore Airlines also makes the list with a long history of luxury amenity kits. Its first class offerings have included products from Lalique or other high-end brands, and even the Star Alliance carrier's business class kits are designed with premium skincare and sophisticated packaging that reflects the airline’s signature attention to detail.

#6177. Can You Redeem Airline Miles For Others? Yes, With Some Caveats

While I love redeeming miles & points for an amazing first or business class flight, one thing that brings me even more joy is being able to do that for friends & family. Along those lines, in this post I’d like to talk about which airline loyalty programs allow you to redeem your points for others. In a separate post, I addressed the topic of whether you can redeem hotel points for others.

While there are some areas where airline loyalty programs are stingy, the ability to redeem miles for others isn’t among those. Generally speaking, airline loyalty programs will let you redeem your miles for anyone you’d like (I’ll note some exceptions below, but unless otherwise noted, that’s what you should expect).

You can almost always do this directly through your frequent flyer program account, by just entering the name of the traveler during the booking process.

Now, it’s important to emphasize that this is for situations where you truly want to gift your rewards to others. Bartering airline miles violates the policies of virtually any airline loyalty program, and your account could be suspended and ticket could be forfeited if you’re caught doing this (and airline auditing departments are quite savvy).

So if you are going to redeem your airline miles for others, make sure you do so in good faith, without expecting anything in return.

To make things as easy as possible, I’d recommend that the person redeeming miles be the one to make the booking, rather than the person being redeemed for. Admittedly the policies do vary by airline:

If you’re making your reservation online, you can always just share your account number and password with someone to make a booking, though that does potentially pose a risk if you can’t fully trust the person (in which case you probably also shouldn’t share miles with them, come and think of it).

I won’t break that down by airline, since there are so many different policies, they sometimes change, and phone agents also often interpret them differently. However, the best way to go about this is to have the person with the miles make the booking. Just make sure you have the full, correct passport or travel document details for the traveler, so that the name matches the ID that will be presented at the time of travel.

There are hundreds of airline loyalty programs out there, and a vast majority of them will allow you to redeem your miles for anyone you’d like. There are some exceptions, though, as some airlines either limit the number of people you can redeem your miles for, or limit the types of people you can redeem your miles for (for example, direct family members).

Most of the programs restricting who you can redeem for are based in Asia. Let me note some of the most common programs with restrictions below. I’d like to emphasize, though, that this list is by no means exhaustive, so if I’ve missed any major programs, please do let me know.

Let me also mention that this is all about the program you book through, rather than the airline you travel with. For example, while All Nippon Airways Mileage Club has restrictions, you could book an award on All Nippon Airways through a partner program without being subjected to these rules.

There are airlines with just a few airplanes that have loyalty programs, so I’ll be focusing on “major” airlines, which I’ll define as airlines with 50+ planes. With that in mind, below are some of the major programs with restrictions:

With some programs that have these restrictions, you simply have to state what the relationship is between the person redeeming and the traveler. In other situations, you may have to provide proof of that relationship.

In some situations this gets tricky, like if we’re talking about same sex relationships that are recognized in some countries, but not others. For example, Korean Air SkyPass will accept same sex relationships as family if they’re recognized in a foreign country (and there’s documentation to prove it). However, since the South Korean government doesn’t legally recognize same sex relationships, a couple in the country wouldn’t be considered family for these purposes, unless they have a legally recognized relationship abroad.

With a vast majority of airline loyalty programs, you’re free to redeem your miles for friends & family without many restrictions. The best practice is to have the person redeeming the miles out of their account make the reservation.

There are a limited number of airline loyalty programs that limit who you can redeem your miles for. In some cases you’re limited to redeeming miles for direct family members, while in some cases you just have to specify redemption nominees, limiting the overall number of people you can redeem for.

What has your experience been with redeeming airline miles for others?

After a six-year hiatus, American Airlines’ most exclusive lounge offering at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) is back in business.

This week, the carrier reopened Flagship Dining at LAX. That’s American’s a la carte restaurant-style experience, which is available to customers flying in its most premium seats.

It had been closed since 2020 but is now open again after a face-lift.

And it also has a new access policy at LAX — and at the two other American hubs that offer the service.

American now offers Flagship Dining at three of its hubs:

At those airports, you'll find the a la carte dining experience is available within its Flagship Lounge, AA's premium lounge that's open to premium cabin passengers and AAdvantage elites taking long-haul flights.

Instead of grabbing food at the buffet, Flagship Dining offers flyers a sit-down meal with table service — we’re talking a full menu with coursed-out dishes, all complimentary.

In the past, the airline limited access to Flagship Dining to passengers flying in its Flagship First cabin on the Boeing 777-300ER or Airbus A321T aircraft.

But as the carrier gets set to phase out its international-style first-class cabin, access to Flagship Dining is opening up to more passengers.

In September, American began allowing passengers in its Flagship business-class cabins to sit for its exclusive dining experience.

If you’re flying out of DFW, MIA or LAX, you can have a Flagship Dining meal if you are:

That change is especially notable at LAX, because it allows business-class passengers to use Flagship Dining on certain transcontinental flights. To get in, you'll need to have a ticket that's marketed as "Flagship" (domestic first-class tickets won't be enough).

Like with any restaurant or airport lounge, space is limited. You can join the waitlist for a table after arriving at the Flagship Lounge in LA, Dallas and Miami.

American used to offer Flagship Dining at John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK). Today, the carrier instead operates its three premium lounges (Greenwich, Chelsea and Soho) in Terminal 8 with partner British Airways.

Meanwhile, its newest Flagship Lounge at Philadelphia International Airport (PHL) features a la carte dining within the main club.

Speaking of American’s “Flagship” product, the end is rapidly approaching for Flagship First.

Nov. 19 will mark the last date AA offers long-haul first-class as a stand-alone product on its 777s.

Those jets are getting refreshed with new interiors, with the airline ditching first-class and adding the highest business-class seat count it's ever offered.

American will phase out Flagship First on transcontinental service in March.

#6175. How To Combine World Of Hyatt Points Between Accounts For Free

The major hotel loyalty programs all have different policies when it comes to combining points between accounts belonging to different members. I’ve already covered the options and policies for Hilton Honors and Marriott Bonvoy, and in this post, I’d like to take a look at the policy of World of Hyatt.

The good news is that World of Hyatt recently introduced a new way to transfer points to others for free, and I’d argue the program now has among the most generous policies in the industry. Long story short, you can transfer or receive up to 525,000 points per year, and this can all be done online, and at no cost. In this post, I’d like to look more closely at the mechanics of Hyatt points transfers.

World of Hyatt offers a generous feature to allow members to transfer points to others at no cost. Let’s first cover the basic rules for Hyatt points transfers:

It’s worth noting that this system is much better than it used to be. Back in the day combining Hyatt points required completing a form and took days, and you could only combine points in order to have sufficient points for a specific redemption. That policy no longer applies.

The process of transferring World of Hyatt points between members online is straightforward. To start, you can either follow this link, or go to your account overview page, and go to the section that reads “Gift your points more seamlessly.”

On the next page, you’ll want to go to the “Gift points or eligible awards” section, and then click “Gift your points.”

There you’ll first want to select how many points you want to transfer, using the slider.

Then on the next page, you’ll need to enter the account information for the account you want to move points to.

Then you’ll just need to confirm the details, and that’s it! Regarding transfer times, reports suggest transfers take anywhere from a few minutes to several days. It does seem like the more points you transfer, the more likely that it takes days for the transfer to go through. So if you are moving a large chunk of points, don’t be surprised if it takes some time.

What are the benefits to being able to combine points between World of Hyatt accounts? On the most basic level, it allows you to combine points so you have enough for an award stay. In other words, if you have two accounts with 15,000 points each, you can combine the points so you have enough for a one night stay at a hotel costing 30,000 points.

Furthermore, if you’re traveling as multiple people and one person has elite status, there’s value to booking the stay out of their account, so that you could take advantage of World of Hyatt Globalist or World of Hyatt Explorist benefits, for example.

However, thanks to the Guest of Honor program, it’s actually pretty easy to give elite perks to friends and family nowadays. For that matter, even Suite Upgrade Awards and Club Access Awards are transferable nowadays.

Lastly, combining points is also considered “activity” for the purposes of keeping your account alive, so it would reset the expiration of points.

World of Hyatt has a great system for letting members combine and share points. World of Hyatt members can transfer up to 525,000 points per year to other members, with limited restrictions. This is possible online, and typically points transfers happen pretty quickly.

There’s lots of value to this, and I’d say Hyatt’s policy is comparable to Hilton Honors for being the best in the industry.

If you’ve ever combined World of Hyatt points, what was your experience like?

#6174. Southwest’s Friendly Airport Agents Can Cost You Money—Change Your Flight In The App Instead

Southwest’s free same-day flight change has a seat fee trap. Airport same day changes make separately purchased seats nonrefundable. Website, app and phone exchanges preserve that payment or trigger a refund, depending on the replacement seat’s price. You can be standing in the terminal, looking at the same replacement flight, but don’t talk to the agent! You’re better off with self-service. Those famously friendly Southwest agents come at a cost. For separately purchased seats: Change at the airport: the original seat purchase is nonrefundable. Website, app or telephone replacement seat costs the same or less: the payment carries over, without any difference refunded. Website, app or telephone more expensive replacement: pay the full new price. With limited exceptions, the old purchase is refunded to the original payment method, separately. You Need To Qualify For A Confirmed Change Free confirmed same-day changes require an available seat, the same origin and destination airports, and the same travel date. Make the change at least 10 minutes before your original scheduled departure. Choice, Choice Preferred and Choice Extra fares qualify, as do Getaways by Southwest vacation bookings. Basic economy customers have to upgrade their fare first even as A-List and A-List Preferred members. Partner itineraries aren’t eligible. Standby is different: you’re waiting for space on an earlier flight, rather than confirming the replacement immediately. Paid seats become nonrefundable when standby clears, including through the app. Elite members on Basic can qualify for standby even though they can’t make a free confirmed change on that fare. List at least 30 minutes before your original scheduled departure using the app or mobile web, or 10 minutes before it in person. A Credit For A Seat Can’t Buy Another Seat One September traveler reported paying about $230 for seats for a trip with their wife, then cancelling and rebooking after a medical emergency. They expected the seat credits to buy new seat upgrades, but the credits were only usable for airfare. Voluntarily cancel at least 10 minutes before original scheduled departure and the seat payment becomes airfare-only credit, for travel completed within 12 months of the original seat purchase. I’ve already covered Southwest displaying different prices to different travelers for the same seat. Customers now need to track the seat purchase separately from the ticket itself, including what happens when either changes. When Southwest downgrades you to a lower seat category, it promises to refund a separately purchased seat to the original payment method. When you exchange two paid connecting seats for a nonstop or direct (same-plane) flight, a replacement costing more than one or both originals triggers only one automatic refund. You need to request the second. Topics on this pageAirline ticketCustomer serviceSouthwest AirlinesMobile app+1 more More From View from the Wing

#6173. Why Singapore Airlines Uses Boeing 787-10s On Short Regional Routes

Boeing built the 787-10 Dreamliner as the largest Dreamliner variant with the shortest range. That makes it well suited to high-frequency, high-demand medium-length routes. Yet, with a maximum range of 7,500 nautical miles (13,890 km), it is still capable of traditional long-haul missions. Singapore Airlines takes its 787-10s in a different direction, using them to fly bizarrely short routes, typically the domain of narrowbody jets.

Singapore Airlines uses its Dreamliner in an unexpected way for several reasons. The 787-10 is a modern jet that replaced the carrier's older widebody aircraft. It has a high-density configuration ideal for ferrying a large number of passengers. It is also fuel-efficient and versatile, making it cost-effective on a range of routes. The answer is also in Singapore Airlines' current fleet, which lacks capacity for short-haul routes with other jets.

Cirium data reveals that Singapore Airlines will fly the 787-10 on 26 routes throughout November. This is for a total of 1,129 operations and over 380,000 seats, with each jet having 337 seats available onboard. The majority of these 26 routes are regional, coming in at less than a third of the 787-10's range.

The table below includes details on the ten shortest 787-10 routes scheduled for November. All of these routes originate at Singapore Changi Airport (SIN):

I Gusti Ngurah Rai International Airport (DPS)

Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport (CAN)

Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport (DAC)

These routes have impressive frequency, showing that Singapore Airlines uses its Dreamliners to move many people over short distances. The fifth-shortest route in November is the carrier's most frequent route that uses the Dreamliner, with 120 monthly frequencies from SIN to MNL. This route is 1,474 miles long and produces almost 60 million available seat miles. That is more than all but two of the routes.

Another exceptionally frequent route included is the third-shortest, taking passengers 876 miles (1,410 km) between SIN and BKK. The airline will complete this route 106 times in November, offering 35,722 seats. This produces over 31 million available seat miles. Meanwhile, it will run daily operations on the shortest route, traveling just 675 miles from SIN to SGN. The over 10,000 seats produce 6.8 million available seat miles.

The 787-10's position within the Singapore Airlines' fleet shows sound logic behind this usage. The carrier lacks narrowbody options that would traditionally operate these short services. Its only single-aisle aircraft are its 26 Boeing 737 MAX 8 jets. These planes have a total capacity of 154 seats split between economy class and business class. This is less than half the 337-passenger capacity of Singapore Airlines' 787-10s. This means the airline's 737 fleet has a total capacity of 4,004 passengers, compared with 9,436 for its Dreamliners. The 787-10 can simply take more of a chunk out of the high-capacity needs within a region packed with huge cities.

The table below shows Singapore Airlines' current fleet, using Planespotters.net data, revealing the position of the 787-10 within it:

On the other hand, all the carrier's widebody aircraft are overengineered for short-haul routes. The most numerous widebody aircraft in its fleet is the A350-900. This jet has a massive range of 8,500 nautical miles (15,750 km), which can extend to 9,700 nautical miles (17,964 km). As a result, the A350-900 has proven effective on long-haul and premium-dense routes. +

The airline often flies its MAX aircraft alongside its larger widebody services to ensure appropriate capacity is deployed on various routes.

Singapore Airlines' Dreamliner configuration has been built with high-frequency and high-capacity needs in mind, making it ideal for moving many people between cities in the Southeast Asia region. Premium passengers have access to 36 business class seats in a 1-2-1 configuration, while the rest of the aircraft is taken up by a massive 301-seat economy cabin. Singapore Airlines has no premium economy class available on this jet. Just one row in this economy cabin is marked as extra legroom.

The table below shows the dimensions of the seats in each of the two cabins, making use of Seat Maps data:

20 inches (51 cm) - expands when armrests are lowered

36 seats is admittedly a substantial business-class cabin, which seems to go against the high-capacity, short-haul philosophy this article has focused on. However, Singapore Airlines uses a staggered layout that squeezes in these seats in a relatively small area. Furthermore, although these seats are lie-flat, they have a shorter pitch and narrower width than what business-class passengers would usually expect.

Despite the prevalence of routes under 2,000 miles (3,200 km), there are still some routes that get closer to the typical way in which carriers use widebody aircraft. In November, Singapore Airlines will fly its 787-10s over 3,000 miles (4,830 km) on four routes. These will be Adelaide Airport (ADL), Tokyo Narita International Airport (NRT), Chubu Centrair International Airport (NGO) in Nagoya, and Osaka's Kansai International Airport (KIX).

Notably, only one of these routes takes the 787-10 outside Asia, and the longer routes within Asia largely reflect Japan's relative isolation from the rest of the continent. The longest of these four routes is to ADL, covering 3,351 miles (5,400 km). Singapore Airlines will complete this route 52 times in November, for a total of 17,524 seats and 58.7 million available seat miles. In 2024, Singapore Airlines marked 40 years of its presence in the city. The airline first flew there in 1984, 18 months after ADL's international terminal opened, using a 747. Along with the 787, Singapore Airlines also uses the A350 for this route, which began in October 2023.

The highest-frequency route, over 3,000 miles, is to KIX, with 90 frequencies across November. This produces 30,330 seats at an average distance of 3,040 miles (4,900 km), producing over 92 million available seat miles. That total is the highest for any Singapore Airlines Dreamliner route.

But it is not the large variant's longest passenger-carrying route of all time.

Relying on a single aircraft type to operate a specific route will always leave an airline vulnerable. This could become a problem for Singapore Airlines with a Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) airworthiness directive coming into effect next month. It covers all 787 variants and was instituted because sealant defects could create a spark inside the jet's fuel tanks during a lightning strike. "The unsafe condition, if not addressed, could result in development of an ignition source within the fuel tank volume," states the FAA order.

The prevalence of this issue and the extent of the problem it will cause remain unclear. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says that 60 of the 170 US-registered 787s fall under the directive, requiring safety inspections. Singapore Airlines' Dreamliners do not fall under this directive, but could be affected if a problem exists for Dreamliners worldwide. The FAA says that impacted jets need sealant inspections where the wings meet the fuselage, along with adhesion checks. FAA predictions put the work for each jet at 34 hours, costing $2,890 per jet. Further costs will be incurred where repairs are required. With over 1,100 Dreamliners worldwide, the problem could cause substantial disruption across global aviation.

Elsewhere in Singapore Airlines' widebody fleet, Boeing problems are causing other issues. Most notably, the carrier has an outstanding order for 31 Boeing 777X jets, placed in June 2017 and February 2021. It has no options for additional purchases. This aircraft family has been long-delayed by certification issues, although Boeing insists that certification and deliveries will finally come in 2027. Given the aircraft's huge size, its arrival should further cement the need for Singapore Airlines to use its Dreamliners on short, high-capacity routes.

#6172. Which Airlines Fly To The Most Destinations? Some May Surprise You

Recently, I wrote a post about the airlines that fly to the most countries. Turkish Airlines wins that title by a long shot, and has a 30+ country lead over the second most “global” airline.

In this post, I want to address a different but related topic — which airlines serve the most destinations? As you’d expect, this is a very different list. That’s because serving a lot of countries is much easier if you’re an airline that has a lot of service in Europe and Africa, given the number of countries there that are in close proximity. It’s one of the reason that US airlines don’t score that well when it comes to absolute number of countries served, despite otherwise being among the biggest carriers in the world.

However, the list of total number of destinations served is a different story…

I don’t think anyone will be surprised by the three airlines that serve the most destinations. As it currently stands:

This makes sense. In terms of fleets, the “big three” US carriers are among the biggest in the world. A majority of their networks are domestic, which is why the airlines don’t rank that high when it comes to total number of countries served, but they do great when it comes to the total number of destinations served. Note that the number of destinations also includes flights operated by their regional subsidiaries.

I don’t think the order above will surprise anyone. United is of course the most global US airline, and has a very impressive route network, including with ultra long haul flights. Meanwhile American is a massive domestic airline, and has a strong network in Latin America and the Caribbean, which is why it doesn’t appear that far behind United in terms of international destinations. And Delta, ummm, gets a revenue premium.

Just in the interest of being thorough, I’m sure some people are curious how many destinations Southwest serves, since it’s an absolutely massive airline in the United States, though doesn’t operate long haul flights. That number is less impressive — it’s a total of 120 destinations, including 104 domestic destinations and 16 international destinations. That’s because the airline is more about depth of service than breadth of service, and doesn’t have a regional subsidiary.

After US carriers, which airlines otherwise top the list of most destinations served? Most people wouldn’t be surprised to learn that Turkish takes that spot, serving 269 destinations, including 46 domestic destinations and 223 international destinations.

What about after that? Here are the next eight airlines (I think this is where some of the airlines may surprise people):

It’s interesting just how different the airlines on the list are. You have the “big three” Chinese carriers, the “big three” European carriers, and then you have Ryanair and Air Canada.

When you put it all together, below is the chart with the 12 airlines serving the most total destinations.

In the interest of being thorough, for those curious about Gulf carriers, Qatar Airways is in first place among them, serving 175 destinations, so it doesn’t quite make the list. Meanwhile Ethiopian Airlines, as Africa’s most global airline, serves 163 destinations

While Turkish Airlines flies to the most countries of any airline in the world, it doesn’t serve the most destinations. Instead that title goes to United, with the “big three” US carriers taking the three top spots. Then Turkish is in fourth place, and is followed by the “big three” Chinese carriers, the “big three” European carriers, and then also Ryanair and Air Canada.

Are you surprised by any of the airlines serving the most destinations?

#6171. Passenger Cut Off From Alcohol Throws Suitcase Off Plane Stairs—Gets 7 Days In Jail

An Uzbekistan Airways passenger demanded more alcohol, cursed at the crew after being cut off, and kept the tantrum going upon landing. Then he threw his own suitcase off the aircraft stairs and kicked it across the ramp. The next day he received a seven day sentence. The 36-year-old Russian man was traveling on flight HY552 from Kuala Lumpur to Tashkent on November 5. According to local reporting on the court proceedings, the senior flight attendant refused his repeated requests for alcohol because he was already intoxicated. He responded by swearing at her and other passengers. Another flight attendant tried to calm him down and received more abuse. Police boarded on arrival in Tashkent. They told him to calm down, leave the aircraft, and come with them to the airport’s administrative building to explain himself. He refused to cooperate and continued swearing. Video of his exit< shows him throwing the suitcase over the side of the stairs. It lands on the pavement with its handle extended. He walks down, approaches the bag, and kicks it away. Usually when a suitcase gets treated like this, the passenger files a claim with the airline. A post shared by Pressa.uz (@pressauz) On November 6, a court in Tashkent found him guilty of petty hooliganism and failing to comply with lawful police demands. He confessed, expressed remorse, and promised it wouldn’t happen again. His punishment was seven days of administrative detention. The court assigned a 440,000 soum (US$36.59) fine to the police noncompliance offense. I’ve covered a United Airlines business class passenger who walked off his own flight when he couldn’t get another drink, and a Russian passenger on flydubai who demanded alcohol and had to be removed by police. Here, we justice acted swiftly. Meanwhile, one of the most popular comments on one posting of the video was “What’s the suitcase brand? It passed the test.” Topics on this pageAdministrative detentionHooliganismTashkentUzbekistan AirwaysFlydubaiKuala LumpurRussianUnited Airlines+4 more More From View from the Wing

He responded by swearing at her and other passengers. Another flight attendant tried to calm him down and received more abuse.

Police boarded on arrival in Tashkent. They told him to calm down, leave the aircraft, and come with them to the airport’s administrative building to explain himself. He refused to cooperate and continued swearing.

You don't have to be a Marriott Bonvoy loyalist to find ongoing value in the (see rates and fees).

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless stands out in the Marriott card suite thanks to its solid lineup of perks, including an annual free night award (certain hotels have resort fees) and elite night credits, for a relatively low annual fee.

Whether you are a frequent Marriott guest or want a few extra perks the next time you stay with the brand, the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless makes sense for a wide range of travelers. Card rating*: ⭐⭐⭐⭐

*Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG's editors and is not influenced by the card issuer.

The is a cobranded card between Marriott Bonvoy and Chase. The card earns Marriott Bonvoy points, which can be used to book free nights at more than 10,000 properties worldwide.

The best way to redeem Marriott points is for free nights at Marriott hotels and resorts. However, you can also transfer your points to airline partners.

Marriott Bonvoy Boundless provides a standout suite of perks, including an annual free night award and automatic Silver Elite status, for a $95 annual fee.

I find it especially impressive that a mid-tier hotel card with a modest annual fee offers such lucrative perks, especially the annual free night award. Certain hotels have resort fees.

Here's a breakdown of the perks included with the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless:

You don't have to go all in on Marriott to get a lot out of having this $95-annual-fee card in your wallet, and that's what makes the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless worth considering.

Related: Marriott Bonvoy elite status 'soft landing' policy: How to requalify for status

The packs a punch for its reasonable annual fee. Here's what cardholders can expect.

Given TPG's November 2026 valuation of Marriott points at 0.75 cents apiece, the 35,000-point certificate is worth $263. This is nearly three times the card's $95 annual fee and is a fantastic benefit, especially since you don't have to spend on the card to earn the certificate.

While the Silver Elite status on the card is the first of Marriott's elite status tiers, it does offer a few useful benefits, such as a 10% points bonus on paid stays and priority late checkout.

If you put at least $35,000 of spending on the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless in a calendar year, you'll earn Gold Elite status. This comes with more perks, such as a 25% points boost and enhanced room upgrade (when available).

For most cardholders, it’s hard to justify putting $35,000 in purchases on the card solely to earn Gold Elite status.

If Gold Elite status is your goal, you may be better off combining the card's 15 complimentary elite night credits with 10 paid nights; this totals 25 elite nights needed for Gold Elite status.

If you're eligible for a business card, you can also pair the 15 elite night credits given by the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless with 15 elite night credits provided by the . These 30 total elite night credits leave you with just 20 nights to earn Platinum Elite.

You can also reach a higher elite status by earning one elite night credit for every $5,000 spent on purchases with the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless.

Related: How to choose a no-foreign-transaction-fee credit card

Given TPG's relatively low valuation of Marriott points, I only recommend paying for Marriott stays with the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless. There are other cards on the market that earn more valuable rewards on dining, gas and groceries.

The best way to redeem your Marriott points is to book free nights at one of the brand's hotels.

Since Marriott uses dynamic award pricing (meaning the number of points needed fluctuates based on demand and availability), you may have to take extra time and effort to strategize for maximum value.

Marriott has an award calendar search function that can help narrow down the best deal for your points. For example, a night at the Moxy NYC Lower East Side in January 2027 could cost as few as 57,000 points per night or as many as 81,000 points per night, depending on when you book.

While we value Marriott points at 0.75 cents apiece, there are ways to get better value.

For instance, TPG lead writer for loyalty programs Katie Genter previously redeemed 112,000 points for a five-night stay at the Courtyard by Marriott Toronto Vaughan for a music festival. Compared against a cash rate of $1,464, she got an impressive 1.31 cents per point from this redemption.

Also, keep in mind that Marriott offers a fifth-night-free benefit. When you book at least five consecutive nights on points, you'll get the night that's worth the lowest number of points for free. This can help you stretch your points for longer trips.

Marriott points are also transferable to nearly 40 airline partners, most at a 3:1 ratio. These include some hard-to-earn currencies, such as Air China PhoenixMiles and Frontier Airlines.

However, unless you have a specific airline redemption in mind and need to top off your balance, transferring is unlikely to be the best use of your points.

Related: Can you mix hotel points and free night certificates for a fourth or fifth night free?

The won't be the perfect fit for everyone. Here are some shortfalls to consider:

The is a premium sibling to the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless. It charges a much higher $650 annual fee (see rates and fees) but provides more benefits for Marriott loyalists.

These perks include higher Platinum Elite status, 25 elite night credits each calendar year toward status and an annual free night award valued at 85,000 points. (Certain hotels have resort fees.)

To learn more, read our showdown of the Bonvoy Boundless versus the Bonvoy Brilliant.

Related: 3 reasons why the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless is worth the $95 annual fee

Currently, new cardholders can earn three free night awards* after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Additionally, they can receive up to $100 in statement credits (up to $50 biannually) after spending $500 on eligible airline purchases (through June 30, 2027).

*Nights are valued at up to 50,000 points each; certain hotels have resort fees.

If you max out the free night awards and earn the statement credits for airline purchases, this bonus is worth up to $1,225 per TPG's valuations.

The current offer delivers decent value for new cardholders. That said, we've seen stronger welcome offers on the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless in the past.

We generally recommend applying when the welcome offer includes at least 150,000 bonus points or at least four free night awards (each valued at up to 50,000 points).

Related: The best credit card welcome bonuses available now

The has multiple competitors. Here are a few to consider:

For additional options, see our list of the best hotel credit cards.

Related: Which credit card should you use for Marriott stays?

I find the to be an excellent choice for a wide range of travelers, from Marriott loyalists who don't want to pay a high annual fee to those who occasionally stay at the brand's hotels and resorts.

This is because you get solid ongoing value from the annual free night award without paying a high annual fee.

Of course, if you're a fierce Marriott loyalist chasing status, a more premium card may be a better choice. And, if you want an option that earns higher-value rewards at a better rate on everyday purchases, you may want to look at a general travel card that earns transferable rewards.

Overall, however, the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless certainly provides enough ongoing value in exchange for its modest $95 annual fee, making it worth keeping year after year.

#6168. Hotel Refills Toiletries From Ketchup-Style Bottles—This Is Why You Can’t Trust What’s In The Shower

This upscale hotel’s housekeeping cart looks ready to dress a hamburger: red, yellow and white squeeze bottles lined up beside the guest supplies. The red one says “Body Wash.” In the shower, the bottles say Klur. Travel journalist Scott Mayerowitz photographed the setup and compared it to the condiments at McDonald’s. He’s glad the hotel is refilling its toiletries. I’m looking at the same photo and wondering how guests are supposed to know what they’re actually washing with. A post shared by Scott Mayerowitz (@globetrotscott) His follow-up photo on LinkedIn shows Klur Repose shampoo, conditioner and body wash in the shower, in the Clary Sage + Lavender scent. My guess, eyeballing the hallway and bathroom, is the Omni Boston Hotel at the Seaport. Readers familiar with the property can confirm or correct that. A September review documents Klur toiletries there, and Klur supplies Omni more broadly. The red squeeze bottle isn’t literally unlabeled. It’s self-labeled. The bottle identifies as body wash. What it doesn’t show is whose body wash. The contents may be genuine Klur, though it seems odd if it were that it would be in a ketchup squeeze bottle. Best case, this looks cheap. They went to the trouble of selecting a branded amenity for the bathroom, then made the refill process look like the back of a burger joint. I’ve Reported This At Hyatt Hotels, Too In May 2025, I wrote about Hyatt Regency San Francisco’s ketchup-style refill jug. A reader photographed an unbranded squeeze container being carried with housekeeping supplies. Guests could see the dispenser in their bathroom, but couldn’t identify the product supplying it. Then, in December, a reader found condiment containers on a housekeeping cart at Hyatt Place Phoenix Mesa. That cart also had a toilet brush beside fresh towels, which didn’t improve the presentation. At Hyatt’s Wild Palms Hotel in Sunnyvale, California, a reader photographed DRIFT bulk toiletries on housekeeping carts while the guest bathroom bottles displayed Jonathan Adler branding. The hotel advertised Jonathan Adler amenities. When One Mile at a Time followed up in January, Ben reported that the labels had been removed from the bulk jugs, and published new photographs. The hotel was still advertising Jonathan Adler. And at the Suining Marriott in China, management there actually acknowledged swapping out cheaper stuff. A guest found FORMETURE products instead of Marriott’s thisworks amenities. The general manager said the owner had changed products to save money. The hotel denied that the replacement was counterfeit, saying it was a legitimate product with quality documentation. It promised to restore the brand standard, and the guest received 8,000 points. Does This Break Any Rules? Klur’s hospitality products are is sold in bulk refill containers. I’d expect those to be used rather than squeeze bottles. Putting a different product into a Klur-labeled bottle could create a misbranding problem. Handling cosmetics under conditions that could contaminate them can violate adulteration rules. And passing off a cheaper product as the promised brand could also run afoul of Massachusetts law against deceptive business practices. Bulk Toiletries Leave More For The Guest To Worry About I’ve been criticizing this move for years. Buying larger containers can reduce packaging (but they can opt for single use biodegradable packaging too). It also lets hotels spend less on toiletries. I’ve shown a Sheraton’s bulk toiletries sitting beside disposable plastic cups, with plastic water bottles elsewhere in the room. They were surely using bulk toiletries out of an ideological commitment to end plastic use. The refill routine adds opportunities to mix up products or introduce contamination. TA 2023 study of 104 hotel soap dispensers in Germany found bacterial contamination in 70.2% of refillable pump dispensers, compared with 10.6% of nonrefillable press dispensers. Bottles that can be opened can be tampered with, and I’ve found supposedly secured dispensers left unlocked. And housekeeping has to remember to fill them. I once returned to the same room at a Marriott Courtyard a week later and found the bath gel dispenser still empty. It had been empty throughout the previous stay, too. You usually discover that problem after you’ve gotten into the shower. Hotels have also given up something that helped sell both the stay and the toiletry brand. I started using Aesop after staying at the Park Hyatt Tokyo. Taking a little bottle home extended the experience and introduced me to a product I still use. Huh, Ben also had a post today about shampoo products. Glad we all seem to like Aesop at least. Bah!

Those are colour-coded : the yellow bottle has sweet peach juice , and the red bottle has thick tomato juice .

(Gary, not on-topic at-all, but did you see the Eisenkot news today? The Times They Are a-Changin’…)

Yes, they could use more attractive containers, but they probably don’t want 3 x 5 liter containers to push around in the cart. So it could actually be Klur that you’re getting…or not.

Unlabeled bottles with chemicals in them violate OSHA HAZCOM rules as well.

Would you prefer the original blue industrial drum with the Chinese shipping label still on it?

I mean this is why I carry my own product

I brought some of Crabtree and Evelyn the Gardeners home from a recent stay.

I can only imagine what bodily fluids people routinely put in these easily-tampered-with jars.

I don’t understand why people only complain! Unite and DO SOMETHING about it.

It’s been so long I can’t remember how I really came upon a company called William Roam who supplies some hotels etc. But I finally found a scent I could tolerate and it is the only time in my near 70 years on the planet I have ever bought a product in a gallon jug to refill my own individual containers. So the little individual bottles we used to find can go along way with some of us to generate more business. I am scent sensitive so rarely would expect to use any of the products left for my use in a hotel room and always go to the trouble to bring my own. Then there are no concerns.

In most hotels, the shampoo and the body wash are the same liquid. I have seen on this couple at two different luxury properties, housekeeping filling both the bottles, the shampoo and the body wash from the same refill jar.

I loathe these refillable dispensers, but that’s the trend these days, so now I travel with my own soap, shampoo, etc so I don’t have to worry about it.

First, I am so happy with the refillable containers. In the shower and–95% of the time–ready to use. And less plastic waste = a great thing! Many times the labels are not easy to read (more still as I get older). I wonder two things about the colored dispensers…easier to explain to staff which one is which with large labels and colors to reduce any mix-ups. And maybe easier to do the refilling. That was my first thought seeing them…bet it is easier for staff to do the actual refilling. (There is a shampoo/conditioner combo I like, but the bottles were made to look unique and are so un-fun to use I no longer purchase their product).

Same, a couple of 100ml bottles weigh nothing. The Omni Seaport bathrooms are nice enough that the refill thing stings more than the product itself. If the brand in the shower matters, it’s usually listed on the hotel’s own site. FWIW a free extension like Directo shows whether booking there direct is cheaper than the OTA anyway. At least the bottles are labelled lol

#6166. Can You Redeem Hotel Points For Others? Yes, You Just Have To Know How

One of the nice things about miles & points is being able to share the gift of travel with friends and family. Now, ideally we’d always be able to go along on those journeys, but there are some situations where that’s not practical, for obvious reasons.

Many people wonder if it’s possible to share their points with others, so they can enjoy a hotel stay. This is a great question, so I’d like to take a look at the policy of each individual program. While hotel loyalty programs in some ways offer more flexibility than airline loyalty programs, this isn’t necessarily one of those areas, as you sometimes have to jump through some hoops. For what it’s worth, in a separate post, I’ve addressed whether you can redeem airline miles for others.

All major hotel loyalty programs have some sort of policy for allowing you to redeem your points for others. In some cases you can directly make a reservation for others, while in other cases you need to transfer your points to another member (at no cost).

Let’s break this down by program. Before we start, let me emphasize a couple of important points:

With that out of the way, let’s get into it…

Accor Live Limitless (ALL) is the one hotel loyalty program that doesn’t let you redeem points for others. However, that’s not necessarily a huge loss. Keep in mind that Accor’s program is revenue based, and every 1,000 Accor points gets you €20 toward a hotel stay folio. You can use this for your own rooms or the rooms of those traveling with you, but you can’t just gift them to a third party.

Choice Privileges allows members to redeem points for reward nights for immediate family members, including a spouse, partner, children parents, in-laws, brothers, and sisters.

You can book a reward night for someone else in one of two ways. If you book through your online profile, be sure to include the name of the guest who will be staying in the room in the “Special Request” field. Alternatively, if booking by phone, ask the reservations agent to include the name of the guest in the notes field of the reservation.

Global Hotel Alliance’s GHA Discovery program is one that I’ve become increasingly intrigued by in recent times, given that it’s associated with dozens of independent hotel groups. GHA Discovery doesn’t have points, but instead, has D$, or Discovery Dollars, as they’re called. Each D$ gets you a dollar off an eligible hotel stay.

What’s cool is that you can actually transfer your D$ to others. A transfer can be initiated through the GHA Discovery app, and you just have to enter the recipient’s membership number and last name. You can begin sharing D$ if you’ve been a member of the program for at least 90 days, and you can perform or receive up to two transfers daily, with a minimum of D$100 and a maximum of D$500 per transaction.

The best way to book a Hilton Honors stay for someone else is to simply transfer points to their Hilton Honors account. Hilton has a free points sharing feature, whereby you can transfer points to another Hilton Honors member. You can transfer no more than 500,000 points to another member, and can receive no more than two million points per calendar year from others. That’s the easiest and most foolproof way to go about this.

One alternative is that you could call Hilton Honors to make a reservation, and explain you want to redeem your points for others. They might be able to book the reservation so that the second guest is listed on the reservation, and it’s documented that this is a gift. However, this might not be quite as seamless as just transferring your points to someone else.

One other option people use is that they’ll make a booking in their own name, and then in the “Add guest names” field on the payment page on Hilton’s website or app, they’ll add the name of the guest in the “Additional guests” field. I’ll talk more about this below — while this might work, it’s not really the official method you should use.

IHG One Rewards’ official policy is that you can book a reward night (either with points or free night awards) for someone else by making a booking via IHG’s website, and then adding an additional name to the reservation. In other words, you’re basically just making a reservation for yourself, with a second guest listed.

There’s also a comments section when making an IHG booking, so I’d recommend writing in that section about your intention to gift an award to someone else.

Marriott Bonvoy allows you to redeem your points directly for others, with some restrictions:

Another option is that Marriott Bonvoy lets you combine points between accounts. You can transfer up to 100,000 points per calendar year, and you can receive up to 500,000 points per calendar year. That’s the biggest restriction, as 100,000 points won’t get you very far, at least for an extended luxury hotel stay. Still, this is a feature I find to be useful.

With World of Hyatt there are a couple of practical ways to redeem points for others. The first is that World of Hyatt lets you outright redeem points or free night certificates for others. This can simply be done by contacting World of Hyatt customer service by phone, and they can process this request, or alternatively, you can transfer reward certificates to someone else’s World of Hyatt account.

If you have World of Hyatt Globalist status, keep in mind that you can also earn Guest of Honor certificates. These allow you to essentially share your Globalist perks with a friend or family member, regardless of whether or not they’re traveling with you. You can apply this either to a stay booked with cash or points, and you can either book the Guest of Honor award out of your account, or you can transfer the Guest of Honor certificate to someone else.

You even get one elite night credit in your own account for each certificate that’s gifted to someone else, after it’s redeemed. This is one of my favorite loyalty perks out there, and it’s a great way to share hotel elite status perks with others.

The other thing to keep in mind is that Hyatt lets you combine points with anyone else at no cost, and this can be done online, through the Hyatt website or app. The person doesn’t have to be related to you, and doesn’t have to live at the same address as you.

The only limitations are that you can transfer up to 525,000 points per year, and can make no more than six points transfers per calendar year. This is probably the easiest option, since the person can just directly redeem out of their own account.

Wyndham Rewards allows members to redeem points for reward nights for friends and family, with no limitations.

This is super straightforward. You can book a stay using points in someone else’s name either directly through the Wyndham Rewards website, or by calling Wyndham Rewards member services. There are no hoops to jump through.

People will often point out “oh, the best way to make a hotel reservation for someone else is to just book it for yourself, and then add the actual guest as the second person on the reservation.” As people view it, the upside is that it lets you earn points, and also share elite perks with others. However, unless explicitly noted above, this isn’t how it’s supposed to work.

It goes without saying that technically you’re only supposed to be able to earn points and take advantage of elite perks if you are actually staying, as the elite member. That’s not to say that this method won’t work sometimes. However, there are some things to keep in mind:

I play by the rules, but there are also plenty of situations where Ford arrives at a hotel before I do (I often take a different and more circuitous routing to get places), and he almost never has issues checking in, and I never even have to go to the front desk.

I’m not making a judgment call here one way or another, but I would only even remotely consider doing this if you and the actual guest both know what you’re doing.

Just about all major hotel loyalty programs let you redeem points for others, though the process varies by program. In some cases you can transfer your points to others, while in other cases you can just redeem a reward for others.

Regardless of which method you choose, just keep in mind that you can’t barter hotel points, and also that your elite perks generally won’t transfer over to others (with the exception of World of Hyatt’s Guest of Honor feature).

If you’ve redeemed hotel points for others, what was your experience like?

#6165. Airport Lounges Just For Singles—A Boarding Pass, A Cover Charge, And A Chance At Finding Love

A traveler wants major airports to open lounges just for single people: pay to get in, meet other singles, and skip the guessing about whether someone wants to be approached. The comments immediately went to (a) married men and (b) Minute Suites. I don’t think the idea is crazy. A boarding pass, TSA screening and lounge access already do some pre-qualifying of potential dates and mates. Add people going to a location where everyone’s signaling they’re open to meeting someone solves the coordination problem. I wonder if it would make more sense to test it inside an existing lounge rather than signing an airport lease for a singles club though. Professional pickleball player Shelby Bates lays out the proposal in an Instagram reel tagged at Atlanta’s airport. She names New York JFK, Atlanta and Los Angeles, proposes an admission fee, and suggests activities, a communal table, speed dating and televisions showing sports (so you already know what team someone likes before making an approach). There needs to be a lounge for single people. A fee to get in. You’re going in there with the mindset that you’re single. Everyone else in there is single. People can approach you, talk to you. She figures she needs to get in touch with an airport CEO. Watch Shelby Bates propose airport lounges for singles But Will The Men Even Be Single Or Just Take Off Their Wedding Bands? Some people love the idea. Others point out that a person can be flying alone without being single, or that the person you meet may live 2,000 miles away – airports are optimizing for long distance relationships. Then there are these: @mauriciopaiz: “Just spent the night in ATL… they should promote the minute suites a bit more 😂” @chinedumikwuakor: “Just gonna be a bunch of married people in that mix lol.” @motobecanegt: “ ‘So, where do you live?’ ‘2000 miles away from you.’ ‘Oooh, we should date.’ ” @mikelyonsphotography: “They are there, it’s called… ‘United Club’.” He then offers to meet her at an airport that weekend. @taliafvr92: “Ugh no!!! I love being single and left alone in the lounge” There’s Already Some Sorting Happening I’ve written about airport lounges and PreCheck as filters for potential dates. A staffed public venue behind security, with cameras and airport police available, has advantages for a first meeting. Travelers have been screened for weapons. Flying and paying for lounge access also let you infer someone’s resources. It’s imperfect information. And a security checkpoint doesn’t get you a full background check (PreCheck is at least going to cover many offenses). Priority Pass would be an interesting addition. If the lounge was accessible that way, it would attract guests whose cards cover their visits. Then the premium credit card it’s attached to serves as a rough signal of creditworthiness (of course Priority Pass also sells memberships directly). The strongest filter would be wanting to meet someone. Earlier this year I wrote about a woman who got an Amex Platinum card to network with rich people in lounges and made “0 connections”. Everyone was eating, scrolling or sleeping. A designated singles space changes that expectation. People still get to decline an approach, and staff would need to deal with anyone who won’t take no for an answer. But you’re no longer trying to work out whether the person beside you wants to talk or finish a presentation. Most lounges might not have enough room, but what about the new 55,000 square foot United Club in Houston? Another benefit is that your flight departure serves as a natural end to that first conversation. Or, if things are going well, missing the flight adds real dramatic tension and a story to tell you grandchildren. People Have Been Trying This For Years Excluding couples and families shrinks the customer base for a lounge. That doesn’t kill the idea if enough people were uniquely motivated by the concept. The operator still needs enough compatible people present at the same time. Age, attraction, orientation, relationship goals and boarding times all winnow down the dating pool. The operator would need rent, buildout cash and a revenue share. They’d cover staffing and food costs. You’re going up against Chase, American Express, Capital One, Airport Dimensions, TAV Services and others bidding for the space. Priority Pass could help supply visits and revenue. But when entry is included with a card, some people will come for the food and drinks and not actually be open to date. People have been trying versions of this for years. In 2015, Lounger proposed matching travelers who had lounge guest privileges with people who wanted to join them. I’ve also covered AirDates, Wingman and the idea of selling introductions through seat assignments. Calls for designated singles lounges were turning up in New York Times airport romance coverage last year. In this reel’s comments, GateF8 showed up to promote its airport connection app. Bates said she’d try it on upcoming trips. I actually think an airport singles event in a lounge would be interesting just for the buzzworthy media coverage it could generate. It may be a collossally bad idea on an ongoing basis but as a one-off it’s surely worth the earned media. #6162. Airbnb Outpaces Rivals With Its Fastest Revenue Growth in 3 Years

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Airbnb guests standing in Cape Town, South Africa.  Airbnb

Airbnb is making its rivals look relatively sluggish. Is it affordability that's kickstarting demand across regions?

Airbnb said Thursday that its revenue grew 19% in the third quarter to $4.9 billion, its fastest growth in three years, outpacing both Expedia Group and Booking Holdings.

The acceleration marks a turnaround from a year ago, when CEO Brian Chesky said at Skift Global Forum that he was “not happy” with Airbnb’s growth. Revenue rose 9.7% that quarter, and growth has accelerated almost every quarter since.

Expedia’s revenue grew 12% in the third quarter, and Booking’s fell 1%, a decline that reflected a $1 billion accounting hit related to a possible FTC settlement over allegedly deceptive practices.

Nights and seats booked, which include homes, hotels, experiences and services, grew 16%. Airbnb didn’t point to a single factor.

It said growth was “primarily driven by strong demand across all regions and continued momentum behind our product roadmap, including search and merchandising, pricing and tools, flexible payments, and sign-

Airbnb said third-quarter revenue grew 19% to $4.9 billion, its fastest growth in more than three years and ahead of both Expedia Group, which grew 12%, and Booking Holdings, whose revenue fell 1% after a $1 billion accounting charge tied to a possible FTC settlement. Nights and seats booked — a combined measure covering homes, hotels, experiences, and services — rose 16%, against 7% room night growth at each of its two larger rivals, though the metrics are not directly comparable. Airbnb attributed the acceleration to demand across all regions and to product work including search and merchandising, pricing tools, flexible payments, and Reserve Now, Pay Later, which it said has extended booking lead times. The expansion beyond homes is showing early traction: Airbnb now lists thousands of independent and boutique hotels in 60 top destinations, up from 20 in May, and said about 35% of guests whose first booking is a hotel come back to book a home. Car rentals, sourced from Expedia's CarTrawler, have become one of its most popular services. AI customer support now runs in 50 languages, resolved roughly 40% of all support issues without a human agent, and cut support costs per booking 17%. Net income rose 35% to $1.9 billion, and Airbnb raised full-year revenue guidance to 16-18% growth from a prior "mid-teens" forecast.
