#6161. Air Algerie Business Class Airbus A330neo Review: Utterly Awful

For the first long haul segment of my Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, my first class quest to Japan, I flew Air Algerie’s Airbus A330-900neo business class on the 6hr50min flight from Montreal (YUL) to Algiers (ALG). I had heard almost entirely negative things about Air Algerie, which intrigued me, naturally! Well, now that I’ve flown Air Algerie I can confirm that everything I heard was true, and then some.

I don’t want to be dramatic — obviously flying business class is better than economy — but honestly, just about everything sucked. On the plus side, the seats as such were fine, but that’s where the good news ends. The food was not good, and took an insanely long amount of time to be served. There were no amenity kits… or menus… or meal choice… or alcohol… or diet soda. If the crew were any more indifferent, they would’ve been invisible.

I wouldn’t fly Air Algerie again unless I absolutely had to, which… I can’t imagine that’ll ever be the case. Honestly, Air Algerie made me yearn for my recent flight on Turkmenistan Airlines, which was at least fun.

Air Algerie is a pretty isolated airline, which perhaps reflects Algeria overall — the country just isn’t interested in visitors, and getting a visa requires jumping through hoops.

So Air Algerie doesn’t have any useful partnerships when it comes to earning or redeeming miles. As a result, booking a cash ticket is just about the only option, unless you’re a frequent flyer with the airline. Air Algerie tends to have rather steep business class fares, despite its lackluster product.

However, I did manage to find a rather attractive one-way business class fare. I booked the following in business class for $1,171 in cash:

10/03 AH2701 Montreal to Algiers departing 4:10PM arriving 5:00AM (+1 day)10/04 AH4000 Algiers to Tunis departing 7:10AM arriving 8:30AM

The first segment was operated by an Airbus A330-900neo, while the second segment was operated by an Airbus A320 that was wet leased from Avion Express.

I had flown into Montreal the same day from Miami (MIA) on Air Canada Rouge, so I had an extended layover. I was at the Air Algerie check-in counter before it opened at 12:30PM, and there was already quite the queue of passengers waiting. Unsurprisingly, and as is very common for North Africa flights, people had a ton of checked bags.

It took me around 30 minutes to get checked in, since there was one counter for business class, and there were half a dozen people in front of me. At first I was asked if I had a visa for Algeria, though I explained I was in transit, which seemed to catch the check-in agent off guard. Air Algerie is clearly targeted at the local community, and doesn’t see much international connecting traffic.

Security was a breeze, and Air Algerie sends its business class passengers to the National Bank Lounge, which is the contract lounge in the international portion of the terminal. I won’t do a full review, but it was actually a pretty pleasant facility, with plenty of seating, lots of natural light, and it wasn’t very crowded.

The food selection was pretty average, with a handful of hot options, plus cheese, cold cuts, etc. There was coffee, tea, wine, beer, and soft drinks. I made the mistake of saving my hunger and thirst for onboard the Air Algerie flight!

My Air Algerie flight was departing from gate A58, with boarding scheduled for 3:10PM, a full hour before departure. I was at the gate early enough to see the inbound aircraft arrive, and goodness, what a stunner it was!

The Montreal route is primarily served by an A330neo with the registration code 7T-VLB, which is in a special livery celebrating the country’s football team. Looking at the plane was honestly the best part of the flight experience, unfortunately.

The boarding area got very full before departure, with lots of passengers in wheelchairs, and lots of crowding around the gate. Boarding ended up starting at 3:20PM, with those needing extra time, as well as business class passengers, being invited to board first.

I can’t describe how excited I was to step onboard, as I always love trying new airlines! I wasn’t fully prepared for the level of indifference shown by every part of the experience, though.

Before I get into this review, I should mention that Air Algerie has recently started taking delivery of Airbus A330-900neos as part of its fleet modernization initiative. However, the airline isn’t just taking delivery of these planes factory fresh, but has also acquired a couple secondhand from Air Belgium, which went out of business in 2024.

Air Algerie maintained the Air Belgium interiors — they also have staggered seats, but it’s a slightly different configuration. I boarded through the second door on the left, and then turned left into the business class cabin.

Business class takes up the entire space between the first and second set of doors, and consists of 30 seats, spread across eight rows, in a 1-2-1 configuration. These seats are from the Stelia Aerospace Solstys line, so they’re typical last generation staggered business class seats. When it comes to the seat details, they have 44″ of pitch, 21″ of width, and convert into 77″ flat beds.

On the plus side, it’s really easy to photograph Air Algerie cabins, since crews are nowhere to be seen. 😉

If you’re traveling with someone, you may appreciate the sets of center seats in odd numbered rows, as these are “honeymoon” seats, which allow you to sit really close to your companion. Meanwhile in even numbered rows, the seats in the center section are further from one another and really close to the aisles, so those would be my least preferred seats in this configuration.

Along the windows, seats alternate between being closer to the aisle and closer to the windows. In odd numbered rows, seats are closer to the aisle. What I particularly don’t like about these staggered seats is just how exposed some of them are to the aisle, as you really have no separation.

In even numbered rows, seats are closer to the windows, and these are the best seats in the house, in terms of offering some separation from the aisle, and an easy view out the window.

I assigned myself seat 6A, the window seat on the left side in the third to last row.

These staggered seats have a console to the side of the seat, and on the side of that is a panel with seat controls, an entertainment controller, and a small armrest.

There’s an exposed storage area above the panel, where you can store things, or even hang the headphones. As you can see, the seat just wasn’t well maintained, and also wasn’t clean, as it also needed a good wiping down.

In terms of charging, the AC power outlet and USB-A outlet were located underneath the seat. There was no USB-C or wireless charging, unsurprisingly.

Looking at the front of the seat, the tray table is stored behind the seat in front, and can be extended by being lowered and then moved over. One of the nice things about these tray tables is that you can angle them away from you, so it’s possible to get up during the meal service.

The entertainment system is in a fixed position and is located above the ottoman. The monitor here was 16″ and was touchscreen, but wasn’t terribly high definition.

As much as there are many aspects of this seat I don’t love, I do like how big the footwell is, which is great for those of us with big feet. It’s not necessarily that comfortable when you’re laying sideways in terms of space for knees, but still, there was a great amount of space here.

One other interesting note is that there were no overhead bins in the center of the cabin, so the overhead bins along the windows got pretty full, since the A330neo doesn’t have huge bins. On top of that, there were no individual air nozzles above seats, sadly. That was a problem on this flight, given how warm the cabin was kept.

All-in-all, Air Algerie’s business class hard product is okay. The cabin maintenance could definitely use some help, but honestly, this is the least of Air Algerie’s problems.

The Air Algerie business class entertainment system on the A330neo is pretty awful. For one, there’s not even a map feature. I’m sorry, I’m not sure the last time I flew an airline with seat back entertainment that didn’t have a map feature. What’s going on there?

The system did have some movies, TV shows, and music, but it was a really lackluster selection.

In total, there were 100 movies and 36 TV shows, but it definitely felt like the number of “popular” options was limited.

The airline presumably went with the cheapest entertainment package available. For example, when it comes to sitcoms, there was one episode of “Fresh Off The Boat,” and it was the pilot episode from 2015. Yikes.

When it comes to Wi-Fi, that’s something that just isn’t offered by Air Algerie. Funny enough, these ex-Air Belgium A330neos have Wi-Fi installed, but the airline just chooses not to use the system. So expect that you’re going to disconnect when flying with Air Algerie.

When it comes to amenities in Air Algerie business class, they were also very limited. The highlight was the pillow and blanket, which were at the seat upon boarding, but not exactly very nicely presented.

Anyway, this was the highlight of the amenities, and while they were nothing amazing, they were at least decent.

Headphones were also passed out well after takeoff, though the quality of them was very poor. This was closer to what you’d expect in economy than business class.

There were no amenity kits, or anything else to speak of. I don’t remember the last overnight business class flight I’ve taken where I wasn’t offered an amenity kit?

Despite the very drawn out boarding process, the crew was nowhere to be seen for most of boarding. Finally at 4:10PM, right at departure time, they came around with pre-departure drinks. There was no “hello” or “welcome onboard,” but instead, just the tray being held out with orange juice or water. At least it was served in glassware… yay?

Boarding this Air Algerie A330neo took an incredibly long time. Every seat was taken (business class seemed to be occupied mostly by operational upgrades plus friends and family). There was just endless confusion, and the crew’s only involvement with things was to occasionally check on people they knew and have chats with them, while everyone else was ignored.

Boarding was also rough because it seemed like the APU was broken, so the cabin was incredibly hot. During boarding, I had asked the flight attendant if I could use the lavatory (I try to do that as a courtesy, even though it showed as unoccupied), and she responded “wait.” I checked with her again some time later, and she again said “wait.” I didn’t end up getting to go before departure… oh well!

Our departure time came and went, and about 20 minutes later I asked a flight attendant if we were delayed. She didn’t understand my question, but after rephrasing, her answer was “no.” The door ended up closing at 4:35PM, 25 minutes behind the scheduled departure time.

At that point the manual safety demonstration began, which was exclusively performed in French and Arabic, and not in English. In fairness, I was probably the only person onboard who didn’t have French or Arabic as my first language. I should also mention there were no safety checks during taxi — some people had their seats reclined, plenty of people still had their (glass) pre-departure beverages, and the guy across from me didn’t even have his seatbelt on.

We began our pushback at 4:40PM, and then at 4:50PM we began our taxi.

While taxiing (and turning a corner), the captain made his welcome onboard announcement at 4:55PM, telling us “this is captain, good morning, taking off shortly.” Okay, we’ll ignore the “morning” part (I’ll assume it just means he’s well rested!), but I assume at Air Algerie the captain is also the one taxiing, right? If so, that’s a lot of multitasking, especially when you’re actively turning.

But hey, credit where credit’s due, this guy was good at turning corners. When we got to runway 24R at 5PM and were cleared for takeoff, we didn’t slowly make the turn and then accelerate. Instead, we started accelerating pretty aggressively in our turn, and were going over 15 knots, while turning at a 90 degree angle. Seriously, check the Flightradar24 data.

We had a very powerful takeoff roll and the captain pulled up on the sidestick as if we were in a fighter jet. The views on the climb out were gorgeous — what a lovely afternoon!

We made a sharp turn after takeoff, and had some nice views of the airport thanks to that.

The seatbelt sign was turned off around five minutes after takeoff. A little while later, we started to get a beautiful sunset view as well.

Dinner was served after takeoff in Air Algerie business class, but my gosh, what a bad and drawn out meal it was. I can deal with bad food or slow service, but bad food, bad drinks, and slow service? BLEH. The first thing to understand is that there were no menus or choices. You’re just served stuff, and it’s a “take it or leave it” situation.

Service began 50 minutes after takeoff, when warm towels were distributed.

Then around 15 minutes later, tablecloths were handed out. These felt more like large, flimsy napkins, than actual tablecloths, but whatever, no biggie.

Another 10 minutes later, the first course was served. The actual food was a little smoked salmon, some egg, some olives, etc. It didn’t taste good at all, but what was worse was the presentation. It’s as if they just threw a bunch of packaging on the tray, and put zero effort into how it’s presented.

I couldn’t help but do their job for them, and make it look a little nicer, because it’s just embarrassing. Oh, and bread is just served by hand out of the basket. Nice.

I kind of loved the Air Algerie branding on the cutlery, but that’s the same cutlery you have to use for the entire meal. For that matter, the cutlery was downright sticky when I removed it from the packaging, so clearly it just hadn’t been cleaned properly.

Drinks were brought out separately from the meal, but they might as well not have bothered. I didn’t realize that Air Algerie is a “dry” airline — it hadn’t even made my list of airlines that are dry. As it turns out, this is only a fairly recent development, as the airline switched to being dry a few years ago.

It’s not only that they don’t have alcohol, but they don’t even have any diet sodas. They have juice or full calorie soda. There was also a huge language barrier here:

“Drink?”“Do you have wine?”“Soda, juice.”“Do you have Diet Coke?”“Coke?”“No, Diet Coke.”“What?”“Coke Zero? Diet Pepsi? Pepsi Max?”*stares blankly*“I’ll have a water, please.”*serves me Sprite*

Another 15 minutes later the main course was served. Again, there was no option, and it seemed to be some sort of a swordfish, or something. As someone who typically loves fish (and orders it way too often on planes), I found this to be way overcooked, dry, and completely tasteless. If you’re not going to offer people a choice of meals, what a random thing to serve!

After an additional pause, the crew came around with cheese plates. I mean, they certainly serve quite a quantity of food, the issue is just that there are no choices, and none of it is actually good. They also don’t actually clear any plates. They just keep bringing more and more food, and if your tray is overflowing, so be it (for the below picture, I had placed the other stuff from the tray over on the side console).

Next up, two whole apples were served, which… I mean, I can’t blame them for the excessive amount of food, serving cheese, fruit, and dessert. But still, this very much feels like an afterthought. I also couldn’t help but wonder if those apples had been washed, given that we’re talking about an airline that serves bread by hand.

Lastly there was a little dessert tart trio. I tried to order a tea without caffeine, but that was a challenge:

“Coffee or tea?”“Do you have any tea without caffeine?”“Coffee or tea?”“Tea please, but no caffeine.”“Coffee?”“Tea, please.”

The entire meal service took close to three hours. Nothing about it was good. The food wasn’t good. The service was terrible. I mean, everything was just so poorly timed. There was never even the offer for more drinks (even just bottled water), and when I did ask, it took them 15 minutes and multiple reminders to actually get some more water.

I just don’t get it. As another example, they served the cheese plates, and then 10 minutes later they came around with more bread, after just about everyone had finished their cheese course. I’m exhausted writing about this. I need a drink.

The Air Algerie A330neo business class lavatory is located at the very front of the cabin. One lavatory really isn’t enough for a full business class cabin plus the crew, so there was often a wait. While there are two lavatories behind the cabin, they’re shared with economy passengers, so there’s usually a line.

The lavatories were fine. Toward the end of the flight they definitely weren’t clean, but to be honest, I’ve seen much worse lavatories on airlines in the region, so I’m hardly going to complain.

By the time the meal service was complete, we had well under four hours remaining to Algiers. So I reclined my seat into bed mode, and tried to get a bit of rest. The bed was okay, and again, compared to the rest of the experience, it was one of the better things.

The issue is how hard it was to actually get rest on this flight. The lights were fully on until after the meal service was complete, so at that point it was under four hours until our arrival in Algiers.

Then the cabin lights were once again fully turned on exactly two hours before arrival. So for those keeping track at home, on a 6hr50min flight, the lights were dimmed for around 1hr50min. I’m not sure I actually slept for a minute. The cabin was really warm, and with the lack of individual air nozzles, I just couldn’t get comfortable.

It absolutely boggles my mind why the crew has to start the pre-landing service a full two hours before landing, when the extent of the breakfast is a single tray with a small side of fruit, a small piece of cake, and a croissant. Seriously, this is what everyone is being woken up two hours before landing for?!

Credit where credit’s due, the drip coffee with milk was drinkable, and perhaps the culinary highlight of the flight. Getting a refill was beyond my abilities, but I sure did savor that one cup!

I understand that North African countries are often known for warm hospitality in a non-transactional setting, where there’s a genuine warmth and generosity to hospitality. Clearly that doesn’t apply in a transactional setting, though, and certainly not on Air Algerie.

I don’t want to say the crew was rude — that wouldn’t be fair, and I didn’t even communicate with them enough to draw that conclusion. They actually seemed to be very nice in how they chatted with their friends who were in the cabin.

As a customer, though, everything about the service was terrible. The crew had no warmth, no attentiveness, they were incredibly disorganized and slow, and the service flow just made no sense. If I were to train a crew on how to provide good service in business class, I’d have them experience this flight, and then have them do exactly the opposite. I think I’ve ragged on them enough.

You’ve gotta love how the refreshing towel has Air Algerie’s logo, and then says “Always caring for you.” If this is what care looks like, I’d love to see what not being cared for looks like!

I was excited when my Air Algerie flight was slowly coming to an end. At around 4:20AM Algiers time the seatbelt sign was turned on, and the crew prepared the cabin for landing. Now, that didn’t actually involve doing any security checks, but they made sure passengers were aware there would be no more service.

We ended up touching down at 4:50AM, and it must’ve been one of the smoothest touchdowns of my life, as you could barely feel it. From there, we had a short five minute taxi to a remote stand, where we pulled in at 4:55AM.

It’s very odd how an airport that has so many empty gates and that’s rather underutilized sends its “flagship” aircraft to remote stands, but whatever.

Upon deplaning, there wasn’t so much as a “goodbye” from the crew. There also wasn’t any priority deplaning for business class, or a separate business class bus. It was quite a long drive to the terminal, and we got there at 5:15AM, where my interesting transit experience started…

I highly recommend flying Air Algerie business class… if you want to be reminded how every other airline doesn’t actually suck that much, by comparison. Air Algerie’s A330neo business class hard product is okay, and is the least of the issues.

The problem is everything else, from the completely indifferent crew, to the unnecessarily drawn out service, to the lack of meal options, amenity kits, menus, diet soda, alcohol, etc., to the subpar entertainment and lack of Wi-Fi… the list goes on and on. And that says nothing of the bizarre elements of the flight, like no English safety demos, no safety checks before takeoff or landing, etc.

What’s sad is that I would’ve actually had a more favorable impression of the flight if they just said “this is a sleeper flight, and we have no inflight service.” Truly, no service would’ve been better than this. I’m happy I had the chance to fly Air Algerie, but you know, I think I’m good for the time being!

What do you make of Air Algerie’s business class?

The Business Platinum Card® from American Express

As High As 300,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

Earlier this year, I was in the middle of a United Airlines status challenge, and I saw an offer for a new credit card with a nice welcome offer that I couldn't resist. I hadn't really played too deeply in the United ecosystem and didn't have any of Chase's United-branded credit cards.

Interestingly, I had a United Airlines debit card in the early 2000's, but that was closed on me when the U.S. passed the Durbin Amendment as part of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act of 2010.

That locked many of us out of lucrative points earning on debit cards.

Anyway, I was excited when I was able to open the (see rates and fees).

Of course, I quickly earned the generous 90,000-mile and 3,000 PQP welcome bonus after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months of account opening and adding an authorized user (no longer available), but I was just as excited to learn I had many perks that came with the card, which I've continued to enjoy this year.

Currently, new cardholders can earn up to 90,000 bonus miles and 500 PQPs: earn 500 PQPs after your first purchase and 80,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening, plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

Here is what comes with the card, which pleasantly surprised me after I got it.

One thing I didn't realize when I signed up for the card was that cardholders get a $200 United travel credit. That came in handy when I needed to book a recent flight to Montana to see my father.

I used the card's $200 annual United TravelBank cash to offset the $488 round-trip ticket cost for my flight from Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) to Bozeman International Airport (BZN). So that trip cost me just $288. Score.

While I haven't used it yet, this card includes up to $150 in hotel credits each year at Renowned Hotels and Resorts for United® Cardmembers. I'm going to try to get a stay in this year to earn that valuable credit.

Here's a potential option that Chase has listed in Bozeman. I stayed at the Kimpton Armory Hotel Bozeman by IHG when it first opened, and it would be a fun hotel to return to this year.

The Quest card also comes with an up to $150 JSX flight credit each anniversary year, up to $180 in Instacart credits each calendar year (through Dec. 31, 2027), and up to $80 ($40 each) in rental car credits each anniversary year for your first and second Avis or Budget rental when you book through cars.united.com. I haven't used any of those perks yet.

I have used the ride-hailing statement credits a few times. You get up to $100 in ride-hailing statement credits with this card (up to $8 monthly from January through November and up to $12 in December; yearly activation required). So far this year, I've used it five times, saving $40.

Finally, there's also a $120 Global Entry, TSA PreCheck or Nexus credit every four years.

Related: United card bonuses: Best-ever offers on 2 of the personal cards

The Quest card comes with some pretty good mileage multipliers. You get 10 total miles per dollar spent on eligible United flights and 4 miles per dollar spent on other eligible United purchases (like onboard food). You also get 2 miles per dollar spent on dining, select streaming services and all other travel.

Note that your mileage earning on Basic Economy and base option tickets may differ from the Quest's standard 10 total miles per dollar spent rate.

I found the miles really added up when I was going for the minimum spend to earn my welcome bonus.

The card also comes with 1,000 bonus Premier qualifying points (PQPs) each year that can give you a head start on earning United elite status. While I was completing my minimum spend, I ended up qualifying for United Silver status, which comes with things like extra-legroom seats starting 24 hours before your flight.

I earned 3,000 PQPs when I opened the card (The current welcome offer includes 500 PQPs after your first purchase). That gave me a huge push toward the 6,000 PQPs I needed for Silver status.

I was able to use my Silver status on that same trip to Montana when I picked Economy Plus seats at check-in.

My Silver status also gives me the possibility for complimentary upgrades, available 24 hours before departure (though they are very few and far between for Silver-level elite status holders).

One of the most incredible perks of holding the Quest card is that it gives you access to additional Saver-level award availability and a discount of at least 10% on award flights.

I was able to spend just 85,000 miles for a one-way flight from Tokyo to Chicago and then on to Newark. That flight could have cost someone without status and the Quest card as much as 450,000 United miles.

In fact, United says my card has saved me 165,000 miles this year alone already.

The Quest card also gets you priority boarding in Group 2, which can mean the difference between being able to bring your carry-on bags onboard or having to gate check them. It also comes with two free checked bags and an annual 10,000-mile award flight discount starting on your first card anniversary.

While I don't love the $350 annual fee on the card, it's partially offset by the generous $200 United travel credit I receive each year. The annual 10,000-mile discount to use toward an eligible award flight is also worth at least $200 to me with my award booking patterns. Together, these two perks alone offset the card's annual fee.

I was mostly interested in the generous welcome bonus when I opened the United Quest Card, but I've been pleasantly surprised by how much additional value I've gotten from it. From the $200 United travel credit to the elite-status boost and the huge savings on award flights, the card has easily earned back the $350 annual fee for me in value.

The Quest card has turned out to be a real winner and will keep a place in my wallet going forward.

#6158. Airbnb CEO: Our Specialized AI Agents Will Handle ‘Every Vertical in Travel’

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Brian Chesky appears remotely at the Skift Global Forum in New York City on September 23, 2026.  Skift

There's been speculation for years about whether Airbnb would launch flights. Such small-minded speculation: Airbnb intends to use specialized AI agents to do every travel vertical. Airbnb Cruise, anyone?

Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky said the company plans to develop specialized AI agents for integrations with numerous partners to handle bookings for "every vertical in travel" in the Airbnb app.

Chesky said partnerships are a key opportunity for Airbnb, which grew for many years mostly organically without such collaborations.

Tags: airbnb, artificial intelligence, earnings, online travel newsletter, travel technology

Skift provides the insights. You make the decisions.

Decision intelligence for travel leaders.

Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky said on the company's third quarter earnings call that Airbnb plans to build specialized AI agents and integrate with partners across "every vertical in travel," with the goal of eventually booking all travel natively inside the Airbnb app. Chesky pointed to car rentals, currently handled through a CarTrawler partnership as a "link off" that sends users to another site, as the model Airbnb intends to replace with native booking on Airbnb. He said the company will sign a large number of partnerships to reach scale, and that native integrations would give Airbnb a greater share of revenue along with responsibility for customer service. Airbnb's shareholder letter said a specialized AI agent will roll out to guests in the first half of 2027. Chesky declined to put a timeline on the broader goal and said he did not want to reveal more of the product roadmap, but he said specialized AI agents will win over generalized ones.

#6157. Air France Jet Turns Toward American Airlines Plane After Takeoff At LAX—Controller Warns ‘Traffic 12 O’Clock’

An Air France Airbus A350 turned left toward an American Airlines jet after takeoff from LAX early Saturday morning, requiring urgent intervention. The controller ordered Air France to turn immediately, and told American to return to 2,000 feet. He warned: “Traffic twelve o’clock. Less than a mile.” The incident is strikingly similar to another close call at the same airport almost exactly a year earlier. Air France Turned Toward The American Plane Both flights took off around 12:15 a.m. on November 7: Air France flight 28, an Airbus A350-900 registered F-HUVK, was departing runway 24L for Papeete, Tahiti. American Airlines flight 1660, an Airbus A321 registered N191UW, was departing runway 25R for Dallas–Fort Worth. These are parallel runways on opposite sides of the airport. Air France was supposed to head west over the ocean, but it began turning left – toward the departure path from the southern runway complex. Controller audio and flight tracking replay “Air France zero two eight heavy. Fly heading of two seven zero immediately.” That means turn west, to a compass heading of 270 degrees. Here’s the warning to American: “Traffic twelve o’clock. Less than a mile. Maintain two thousand.” American had already climbed above the altitude the controller wanted it to hold. The controller had to turn Air France away while bringing American back down to 2,000 feet. The FAA departure instructions in effect that day direct aircraft leaving runway 24L to begin on a heading of 251 degrees, proceed DLREY followed by ENNEY. The route continues broadly west. The Air France A350 shouldn’t have made an early left turn into the other departure stream. The controller had told Air France to “climb via” its assigned departure. That means following the published route and its altitude restrictions. He challenged the crew about turning to a heading, and repeatedly asked which departure they’d been instructed to fly. “Air France zero two eight heavy. Thank you very much. Possible pilot deviation. I have a number for you to call when you’re ready.” Air France flew a turn that didn’t match its assigned departure, and it’s not clear yet what happened: a wrong route loaded into the flight computer? a manually selected heading? a misunderstanding in the cockpit? How Close Was This? Simple Flying emphasizes 400 feet of vertical separation. But there was nearly a mile between the two planes. This was serious. Two departing aircraft had converging paths, the controller issued a traffic alert, and ordered an immediate turn while restricting the other aircraft’s altitude. But they didn’t come within 400 feet of colliding. I haven’t seen it reported that there was a collision avoidance resolution advisory. The departure route wasn’t followed, and the cockpit checksprevent the deviation from developing into a traffic conflict. The controller saw the conflict, issued instructions to prevent a problem, and both crews followed those instructions. Almost The Same Thing Happened Last Year On October 31, 2025, an ITA Airways Airbus A330neo departing Los Angeles for Rome turned left toward an American Airlines Airbus A321 bound for New York. It was the same pair of runways with ITA departing 24L, and American departing 25R. The controller ordered ITA right to heading 270 and told American to stop its climb at 1,500 feet. ITA’s crew also received a possible pilot deviation notification. There was also the December 2025 Houston encounter between Volaris El Salvador and a United Express regional jet. In that case, the Volaris crew read back a left turn correctly but turned right, toward the other departure. The United Express crew reported a collision avoidance advisory. I was reading about this incident on X and I found your blog by searching for this specific phrase: ““Fly heading of two seven zero immediately.”

As a non-native English speaker I found myself often struggling very much to understand air traffic controllers (in media, luckily I do not fly myself) because the radio communications are often unclear but also the phraseology is quite specific. What was this instruction supposed to mean? Doesn’t “fly heading of X” mean that pilot should turn X?

Again, not a pilot and not a native speaker, so excuse my ignorance please. Everyone in the thread was piling on the French pilot but a couple of people did bring this up, which made me search for an answer.

This keeps happening at LAX, different carriers, not great. It’s no longer merely a coincidence or ‘distracted pilots’… something isn’t right, and they need to address and resolve it.

Too many aircraft , too many flights , too little leeway . Reduce all flights by 75% , and stagger take-offs for one every 15 minutes .

I have recommended this for many years , yet they ludicrously keep adding more flights .

Seems like the American flight should have seen the Air France traffic if it was at 12 o’clock and at a slightly higher altitude. It was LAX so likely not IMC

Albert – no. Just no. Here are some crayons. Go color or something. Let the adults deal with this.

LAX has, on average, about 800 daily departures, or in excess of 290,000 takeoffs per year. Within the past five years, there have been FOUR highly-publicized incidents of a crew turning the wrong direction immediately after taking off in LAX. So it’s happening roughly 0.00137% of the time. Your idea is ludicrous to put it kindly.

As someone who’s flown into and out of LAX for decades, the problem almost always comes down to a pilot error. If you expect to depart runway 25R, and you set up the “box” (the FMS computer) for it, the route it “grabs” includes the early left turn used by 25R. Now, during taxi out, ATC gives you runway 24L for departure.

Every plane is a little different, but if you follow the correct, prescribed steps in the correct order needed – as you make the changes, the box will grab the associated route with 24L, and give you a course that’s nearly straight ahead instead – as it’s supposed to do. But if you short-cut the steps (just swap the runway, instead of reloading the departure procedure too) and it’s possible to get the 25R route with the 24L runway. That’s likely what happened here. The flight management computer will direct the southbound turn from the northern set of runways.

It is a mistake that becomes likely when a crew is 1) tired (long-haul flying is fatiguing by its very nature, even at the beginning of a flight), 2) tasked with a higher workload because they now must obtain new takeoff data because they got a different runway, and 3) faced increasing workload-management issues as they now received taxi instructions contrary to what they expected… as they are going to a new runway. Heads go “down” (one works on the box and the data, while the other makes sure to follow the correct taxi instructions), cross checking can get missed, and an error can be made.

The solution? No – it’s not to cut 75% of the system. That would make things LESS safe by reducing proficiency and experience. The industry would become less attractive, so fewer would aspire to it. The airline’s new pilot candidate aptitude would drop. Resources to improve safety would evaporate (which created, over the past few decades: GPWS, TCAS, CPDLC, vastly improved on-board weather radar, safety management programs, etc. etc. etc.). The solution is to continue to invest in pilot and ATC training. To insist on two pilots in the flight deck, and adequate training and staffing for ATC.

No aviation system can 100% eliminate all threats, errors, and mistakes (short of just grounding all flights, paving over all airports, and scrapping every plane in existence). What Albert doesn’t seem to realize is what we saw here was the system WORKING. When a mistake happens by one airline crew (the Air France flight) ATC was paying attention, and had the situational awareness to quickly address it. And the American crew was also trained, ready, and capable of quickly handling a non-routine instruction to get out of the way.

When mistakes happen – and they always will – the system needs to quickly catch it and provide a correction before things turn disastrous. That’s how it’s supposed to work, and that is exactly what it did.

PilotPaul – Lindbergh did OK whilst flying solo and without a FMS computer , because he did one take-off at a time . The problem here is too many take-offs and landings at one time .

This is not the elevated experience that LAX’s guests are accustomed to.

So you are equating a rickety, slow, experimental flight that took 33+ hours to complete – that same close to failure on several occasions during the flight (including the takeoff) – as the standard we should strive to duplicate?

PilotPaul – Lindbergh would not have allowed helicopters to cross flight paths at DCA . Lindbergh’s answer would be to reduce them and get a handle on it .

ha ha Wikipedia hates Simple Flying, which is mentioned in Gary’s article above! In fact there is Wikipedia litigation ongoing. I wonder if people are allowed to comment because Wikipedia is a website that anyone can edit??? https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Arbitration/Requests/Case/Airline_destinations/Evidence

#6153. Qatar’s Tourism Recovery is Coming by Road, Not Air

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Qatar markets.  Qatar Airways

Qatar’s visitor numbers are recovering on road traffic across the Saudi border, while air arrivals keep falling. Drive-in visitors tend to make shorter trips, which limits how much they can do for hotels.

Qatar’s tourism recovery from the U.S.-Iran war is running on road traffic across the Saudi border, a Skift analysis of Qatar Tourism data shows. .

International visitor arrivals in October totaled 336,000, down 10% from the same time last year, according to Qatar Tourism’s monthly arrivals data. September’s arrivals were up 1%. Both are a sharp turnaround from March, when arrivals fell 82% year over year to 63,000.

Qatar received 2.95 million visitors in the first 10 months of 2026, down 24% from 3.9 million in the same period last year.

Road is the only part of Qatar’s arrivals that is growing. Land arrivals, which all come through Qatar’s sole land border with Saudi Arabia, rose 18% year over year in October. Air arrivals fell 19%, registering an eighth straight month of decline.

That matters for hotels and for tourism revenue. Visitors flying in from long-haul markets typically stay longer and spend more than weekend drive-in gu

Qatar's tourism recovery from the U.S.-Iran war is being carried by road traffic from Saudi Arabia, a Skift analysis of Qatar Tourism data shows. International arrivals reached 336,000 in October, down 10% year over year, and 2.95 million in the first 10 months of 2026, down 24% from 3.9 million a year earlier. Land arrivals through Qatar's only land border rose 18% in October and now make up 31% of all arrivals, up from 24% a year earlier. Air arrivals fell 19%, an eighth straight monthly decline, after collapsing 90% in March. Shaza Doha general manager Siddhartha Chowdhry said several pre-war source markets have yet to return, citing travel advisories, reduced airline seat capacity, higher travel insurance costs, and weaker traveler confidence. Hotel occupancy in September was 61.5%, down three percentage points year over year but well above April's 44.5% low, with RevPAR down 4%. Sea arrivals have been near zero since March, and the new cruise season is a test of whether ships return. Qatar is again leaning on events — MotoGP in early November and F1 from November 27 to 29 — after last year's F1 weekend drove ADR of about $241 and roughly 92% occupancy on its opening Friday. ValuStrat's Saad Lodhi expects cooler weather and F1 to lift performance but warned against counting on a repeat of last year's peaks.

Can a low-cost carrier ever really be premium? Frontier Airlines certainly seems to think so.

In recent years, the airline has added front-of-plane seating with extra legroom and blocked middle seats, combined its extras into fare bundles and even announced plans for first class.

You can pay for those bundles with Frontier Miles, too. The top-tier Business Bundle is the closest thing Frontier has to a premium experience, with just about every bell and whistle the airline offers.

The catch? It usually costs more than double the miles of a bare-bones Basic fare.

Are the extra miles worth it? I put it to the test by taking one flight on a Basic fare, then another on the Business Bundle.

Related: Frontier wants to be an airline you'd choose to fly. Will first class and new perks do the trick?

Frontier sells a no-frills Basic fare plus three bundles that add bags, seats and flexibility, and you can book any of them with cash or miles.

The amounts below are minimum one-way prices per traveler. Taxes and fees start at $5.60, and miles can only be redeemed for a bundle at the time of the original booking.

Related: Flying Frontier Airlines? You can now redeem miles for seats, bags and other perks

My first Frontier flight was from St. Louis Lambert International Airport (STL) to Denver International Airport (DEN). I paid for it with the 5,000 miles I'd earned from Frontier Airlines' Super Bowl promotion earlier this year (offer no longer available), so only the $5.60 in taxes and fees came out of my pocket. Transferring Rove miles to Frontier is also an easy way to top up your balance.

You really can't argue with that value for a two-hour flight. The trade-off, as anyone who's flown a low-cost carrier will know, is everything you don't get.

A Basic fare only covers a personal item. That turned out to be the biggest frustration of my Frontier experience, as this won't be a realistic option for folks traveling for longer than a day or two.

Boarding in Group 5 as a Frontier Miles member wasn't an issue, and the process was more orderly and civilized than I expected. With nothing to put in the overhead bins, there wasn't a need to board early anyway.

I just found my seat all the way back in row 27 (I couldn't select it myself) and settled in.

The flight itself was uneventful and punctual, which on a low-cost airline is really about all you can ask for.

Related: How to use credit cards to defeat basic economy

For my second flight, a short hop from Denver to Kansas City International Airport (MCI), I booked the Business Bundle, and the perks landed before I even got to the airport.

Being able to select Seat 1A during booking sure was convenient. True to the UpFront Plus promise, the seat next to me was empty.

Frontier's new 2-2 first-class seats had not yet entered service when I flew, so my aircraft retained the existing 3-3 layout.

I boarded in Group 1, right behind preboarding, and didn't need to pay extra for luggage. The bundle included a full-size carry-on and two checked bags, each weighing up to 50 pounds, which was far more than I needed for this short trip.

What you won't get, in any bundle, is complimentary food or drinks.

Frontier doesn't include food, drinks or lounge access with its bundles, so anything you want on board comes at an extra cost, and it was a sobering reminder that this was still a low-cost carrier.

Related: Frontier makes it easier to earn top-tier elite status in 2027 but cuts earning rates for basic fares and noncardholders

Unless I needed to pack a lot of luggage or particularly valued the extra space of an UpFront Plus seat, I don't think I'd spring for a Business Bundle again, whether I was paying with cash or redeeming Frontier miles.

For even the cheapest redemptions, the Business Bundle costs 8,000 more miles than a Basic fare, which is more than double the price. For a short domestic flight with nothing to eat or drink, that's a lot more miles.

Frontier's Business Bundle is not a bad product. It's just that a Basic fare for as little as 5,000 miles at that price is terrific value, and that's a tough act to follow.

For most travelers, the sweet spot is probably the Economy Bundle. It starts at just 2,000 more miles than a Basic fare and fixes the thing I missed most on my first flight, a proper carry-on, while making your booking far more flexible.

I'd be happy with that for my next Frontier flight.

Related: Frontier Airlines' planes set for big upgrade: Starlink Wi-Fi coming in 2027

So, can a low-cost carrier be premium? After flying both fares back-to-back, the Business Bundle felt more like paying for convenience, baggage and personal space than a genuinely premium experience.

Your own experience will depend a lot on the route, the dates and how much luggage you need to take, and Frontier's lowest award rates won't always be available.

Unless you need two checked bags or place a high value on the extra space of an UpFront Plus seat, the Economy Bundle is probably the better balance of price and useful benefits.

#6149. Finnair’s Cheap Avios Sale Offers A Shortcut To Status On American Flights And Access To Flagship Lounges

Finnair is selling 200,000 Avios for $2,170, and throwing in 20,000 points towards elite status. Those Avios can buy business class awards on Finnair, or move over to British Airways and Qatar Airways. And the status points can help you get into American Airlines Flagship lounges even when you’re flying domestic coach. The purchase alone gets you Finnair Silver, which is oneworld Ruby, and I don’t see much value in chasing Ruby. You get some airport priority on American and Alaska and a free checked bag. Finnair Gold, which is oneworld Sapphire, comes with lounge access including business class Flagship lounge access. The latest Frequent Miler on the Air episode walks through the sale and ways to leverage it. One Mile at a Time covered the offer when it launched. I’ve written about buying Finnair points to earn oneworld status since November 2020, and covered another version in December 2021. Those offers could get you all the way to Sapphire or Emerald without flying. This one is less generous for status, but the redeemable points are much more useful now that Finnair uses Avios than they were back then. What The Avios Cost Now The sale runs through November 16, 2026, ending at 4:59 p.m. Eastern. You need to have joined Finnair Plus before October 30 and have at least 50 Avios in your account. The purchase allowance has been reset for this offer: you can buy up to 200,000 even if you already hit the normal annual limit. The discount reaches 50% at 85,000 Avios. The best dollar pricing is available on purchases of 100,000 or more: 1.085 cents per Avios, before card rewards or shopping portal earnings. The purchase also generates tier points equal to 10% of the Avios bought. The podcast described paying in Japanese yen for about 1.06 cents apiece, then earning 3 points per dollar on an Atmos Rewards Summit card’s foreign purchases category. That yen price is no longer available and dollars are now the better deal. Purchases are processed by Points.com, not as airline tickets. Use a card with a strong return on otherwise unbonused spending. Finnair’s milestone rewards add another layer of benefits. A Basic member crossing 12,000 tier points receives 3,000 extra Avios. Starting at zero, and assuming that milestone hasn’t already been earned: Purchase Dollar Cost Avios Including Milestone Tier Points 120,000 Avios $1,302 123,000 12,000 150,000 Avios $1,627.50 153,000 15,000 200,000 Avios $2,170 203,000 20,000 The 120,000-point purchase works out to about 1.059 cents per Avios after the milestone. That’s slightly cheaper per point than buying the maximum. Existing Gold members don’t receive this Basic-tier milestone (Finnair only awards milestones within your own tier). Frequent Miler also flagged Rove at 1 mile per dollar and Extrabux at 1.6%–2% cash back as potential shopping portal optins to start with when buying the points. $1,302 would earn 1,302 Rove miles, which are also transferable to Finnair. Ruby Isn’t The Status I’d Spend Money Chasing Silver requires 15,000 tier points (not 20,000 as some discussions suggest, which is actually a separate milestone awarding two Finnair lounge passes). Buying 150,000 Avios already earns Silver from zero. Ruby gets you business class check-in and some seating and waitlist benefits. On American, it also means a free first checked bag and Group 4 boarding. Finnair Gold gives you oneworld business class lounge access, along with additional baggage and priority services. And because the status comes from Finnair rather than American or Alaska, American permits Flagship lounge access on eligible domestic trips as well. You can bring one guest. It doesn’t include Flagship Dining. You also get Admirals Club access and Alaska Lounge access when flying either airline. Gold also comes with four Finnair upgrade benefits covering one short-haul economy-to-business upgrade each or U.S.–Helsinki would use all four, requiring upgrade availability. You can also exchange all four for a two-for-one Finnair Classic economy or premium economy award. How To Get From This Sale To Sapphire Finnair Gold requires 45,000 tier points. Starting from zero, buying the maximum gives you 20,000. You can then exchange 22,500 Avios for 7,500 tier points. That leaves you with 27,500 tier points, 17,500 short of Gold, and 180,500 redeemable Avios if you received the Basic milestone. Finnair allows one exchange per personal tracking period, at three Avios per tier point, with a 500-tier-point minimum and a €10 online fee. The ceiling depends on your status when you exchange: 7,500 tier points for Basic or Silver, 22,500 for Gold, and 40,000 for Platinum or Platinum Lumo. An existing Gold member has a much easier renewal calculation. Buying 200,000 Avios generates 20,000 tier points, and converting 67,500 Avios adds 22,500. That’s 42,500 towards the 45,000 needed, leaving just 2,500 to earn if you started the period at zero. You’d retain 132,500 purchased Avios. For someone starting without status, American flights can fill the 17,500-point gap. Finnair’s earning chart for business class, including domestic flights with Finnair Silver status: J, C and D earn 250% of distance before the Silver bonus, or 275% with it. You’d need about 6,364 flown miles to generate 17,500 tier points. R and I earn 150%, or 165% with the Silver bonus. You’d need about 10,607 flown miles. Check your account’s personal tracking period before doing any of this. It isn’t the calendar year, and buying points or reaching Silver doesn’t restart it. Purchase, conversion and remaining flight credit need to fall in the same period. Once you reach Gold, the status lasts for the rest of that period plus the following 12 months. You Can Use Credit Card Points For The Final Top-Up You don’t have to buy Avios to use the conversion feature. If you’re 3,000 tier points short of Gold, you can transfer in 9,000 Avios and exchange them, paying the €10 online fee. Capital One transfers directly to Finnair at 1:1. Or transfer a bank currency into British Airways, then move those Avios into Finnair. Qatar Avios can go through British Airways to reach Finnair, too. Finnair’s current linking rules require an account at least 30 days old, matching names and email addresses, and two-factor authentication. That’s important even for getting the 50 Avios needed for the sale since an account opened shortly before the October 30 cutoff may qualify for the promotion but still be too new for an Avios-program transfer. The Avios You’re Buying Are Valuable, Too I covered Finnair’s improved award opportunities in May 2024. You can redeem through Finnair or move Avios 1:1, without a transfer fee, to British Airways and onward to Qatar or other Avios programs as well. That’s 42,500 towards the 45,000 needed, leaving just 2,500 to earn if you started the period at zero. You’d retain 132,500 purchased Avios. For someone starting without status, American flights can fill the 17,500-point gap. Finnair’s earning chart for business class, including domestic flights with Finnair Silver status: J, C and D earn 250% of distance before the Silver bonus, or 275% with it. You’d need about 6,364 flown miles to generate 17,500 tier points. R and I earn 150%, or 165% with the Silver bonus. You’d need about 10,607 flown miles. Check your account’s personal tracking period before doing any of this. It isn’t the calendar year, and buying points or reaching Silver doesn’t restart it. Purchase, conversion and remaining flight credit need to fall in the same period. Once you reach Gold, the status lasts for the rest of that period plus the following 12 months. You Can Use Credit Card Points For The Final Top-Up You don’t have to buy Avios to use the conversion feature. If you’re 3,000 tier points short of Gold, you can transfer in 9,000 Avios and exchange them, paying the €10 online fee. Capital One transfers directly to Finnair at 1:1. Or transfer a bank currency into British Airways, then move those Avios into Finnair. Qatar Avios can go through British Airways to reach Finnair, too. Finnair’s current linking rules require an account at least 30 days old, matching names and email addresses, and two-factor authentication. That’s important even for getting the 50 Avios needed for the sale since an account opened shortly before the October 30 cutoff may qualify for the promotion but still be too new for an Avios-program transfer. The Avios You’re Buying Are Valuable, Too I covered Finnair’s improved award opportunities in May 2024. You can redeem through Finnair or move Avios 1:1, without a transfer fee, to British Airways and onward to Qatar or other Avios programs as well. Jet fuel above $4 a gallon has reset the math on every airline plan for 2027. Next week, the executives making those calls spend a full day at the TWA Hotel at JFK. Here is how to spend yours, by role.

JetBlue President Marty St. George said this week that airline pricing has yet to find its equilibrium as costs keep climbing. On Wednesday, November 11, he takes the stage in conversation with Brian Sumers, Editor of The Airline Observer. His session closes out Skift Commerce Summit and kicks off Skift Aviation Forum 2026, which brings the executives setting 2027 plans to the TWA Hotel at JFK the next day.

For the thinking behind the program, read Five Decisions in the Room. Here is how to spend the day by role.

Skift Aviation Forum 2026 convenes at the TWA Hotel at JFK on November 12, preceded by Skift Commerce Summit on November 11 at Apella by Alexandria, with a program built around one condition: jet fuel prices doubled in 2026 and airlines have not yet found a fare level that covers the increase. JetBlue President Marty St. George, in conversation with Brian Sumers of The Airline Observer, said this week that airline pricing has yet to find its equilibrium as costs keep climbing; his session closes the Commerce Summit and opens the forum. The agenda is organized by executive role. Commercial and revenue leaders get American Airlines' Nat Pieper on premium and loyalty as American slows growth for 2027, and IAG's Luis Gallego on holding margin through a fuel spike. Network and fleet leaders get Breeze Airways' David Neeleman on growth and mergers, Embraer's Arjan Meijer and Porter's Kevin Jackson on whether smaller jets ease a delivery-slot squeeze running to roughly 2033, and Airbus North America's Robin Hayes. Loyalty and distribution sessions address programs now worth more than the airlines that own them and AI shopping tools that compare every program in seconds, with Agoda's Damien Pfirsch, Delta, Allianz Partners, Flying Blue, and oneworld. Airports and operations sessions feature Los Angeles World Airports, Paris-Charles de Gaulle, Air Canada, American Express Travel, and Sara Nelson of the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA on labor's place in the margin story as Ryanair pushes pay freezes.

#6144. Tourism Heads to COP31 Wanting Results, Not More Pledges

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: UN Climate Change - Kiara Worth

Five years after the Glasgow Declaration, tourism has plenty of climate commitments but little shared proof of what they’ve achieved. The industry is still split on whether better measurement or faster action should come first.

COP31, the world’s annual marathon of climate talks, kicks off next week. After years of planning climate action, tourism operators told Skift that they now want to see the receipts.

The 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference will take place in Antalya, Türkiye, from November 9 to 20. Co-hosted with Australia, this fresh round of climate talks is being billed the implementation COP, after parties ultimately failed to agree on a path forward last year in Belém, Brazil.

The Brazilian COP30 presidency promised to publish plans for moving away from fossil fuels and protecting forests before the next round of talks.

The voluntary roadmaps, released Tuesday, are designed to help policymakers implement their existing climate commitments through national policies, investments and measurable results — and should indicate some of the focus of the forthcoming talks.

The newly published fossil fuel roadmap, building on the

COP31 opens in Antalya, Türkiye, from November 9 to 20, co-hosted with Australia and billed as the "implementation COP" after parties failed to agree on a path forward at COP30 in Belém. Tourism gets a thematic slot on November 18 for the third year running, this time inside a day on human and social development, and the sustainability executives Skift spoke with said they want evidence of change rather than new pledges. Radisson Hotel Group's Sven Wiltink pointed to inconsistent measurement of emissions, water, energy, and waste, arguing that without common metrics "comparisons are meaningless and claims remain unverifiable." Intrepid's Susanne Etti said the sector needs electrification and falling emissions, not more commitments, targets, or frameworks, and that resilience, adaptation, and loss and damage funding have become more urgent after a year of extreme heat, wildfires, and flooding. Booking Holdings' Danielle D'Silva said the industry can do more on both adaptation and emissions reductions. COP31 also marks five years since the Glasgow Declaration on Climate Action in Tourism, which has drawn more than 900 signatories; revised operational guidelines will be released at the conference, with co-author Jeremy Smith saying the aim is to lower the measurement and reporting burden and bring in companies that stayed out.

#6142. American Airlines Updates Vouchers For Stranded Passengers—But Tells Employees There May Be Fewer Hotel Choices

American Airlines is updating how stranded passengers get hotel rooms, meal credits and rides during flight disruptions. An internal November memo I reviewed lays out automatic offers for eligible overnight delays and a new way for agents to arrange Uber rides without making passengers download the app. It also warns that employees may see fewer hotels to choose from. Getting passengers out of the customer service line and into a room sooner is great for getting sleep. On a recent American Airlines flight from New York to Austin that was cancelled after a long delay I didn’t even bother getting into the long line at the gate for a room voucher, I just booked something myself nad went on my way. What American Is Changing The update covers American’s Hotel, Meal and Transportation system, which employees call HMT. October 26: standalone meal credits. Agents can issue food and beverage credits for individual reservations affected by qualifying delays, cancellations and missed connections. The system uses flight information to evaluate eligibility and tells agents what qualifies. October 27: automatic offers for eligible overnight delays. The system sends hotel offers and applicable food and beverage credits when its eligibility and automation criteria are met, reducing the need for an employee to initiate the offer. Planned Uber Central rollout. At participating airports, authorized agents would arrange a ride on the customer’s behalf through the same system. The passenger receives a text message or WhatsApp link to start the ride, without downloading Uber. This should now be available but I haven’t seen passenger reports of the broadly available rollout yet (though customers reported it in limited release previously). Hotel inventory changes, date undetermined. American is changing the hotel inventory feed and selection process. Employees are told they may see fewer hotel choices. Automatic Vouchers Already Exist American has been working on this for years. I covered the electronic hotel and meal system in 2019, when agents still had to qualify customers and trigger offers. American was already describing automatic hotel, meal and transportation vouchers in 2025. This spring, they added meal issuance for an entire flight at once. In June, automatic meal vouchers expanded beyond elite members to all AAdvantage members. American’s January app changes already brought disruption assistance together: Their published customer service plan promises, upon request, an approved hotel for an overnight disruption they cause away from your city of residence, transportation there and back, and a food and beverage credit after a qualifying delay of at least three hours. The standard meal voucher I’ve been covering is $12. American recently renamed it a “food/beverage credit” because calling it a meal voucher led passengers to expect it to pay for a meal. How The Uber Change Works American already offers Uber vouchers. The change lets an agent arrange the ride for the passenger. Uber Central supports rides paid for by the business, with trip details sent to the customer. However, American’s instructions still put the hotel shuttle first, followed by an Uber voucher. Uber Central is for exceptions when those options don’t meet the customer’s needs. One passenger reported being at Washington National when agents refused Uber vouchers because a hotel had a shuttle even though it wasn’t running at 1 a.m. Fewer Hotel Choices Isn’t Great The memo’s most concerning sentence is: Frontline teams may see fewer hotel choices displayed than they are accustomed to seeing. Being able to choose a hotel matters. I’ve covered passenger complaints about unsuitable rooms and missing shuttles. Here’s a passenger who said the hotel floor was so dirty they spread sheets over it. If American can’t provide an approved hotel voucher, its customer service plan promises reimbursement of reasonable hotel costs. Its conditions of carriage also say reimbursement isn’t guaranteed when you book directly without written authorization. Credit card trip protections may reimburse required hotel overnights as well. AC gave us $16/person for ‘meals’ after a 4 hour delay on an ex-SFO flight a couple of years ago. You’d need pretty close to double that to cover an average meal at SFO. We had already eaten, as delay was not known until we were boarded. So we received them after we were told we needed to de-board. So what did we do. Took our $64 to a place where we could get snacks. What did we net for a single $16 voucher? A couple of bags of snacks (chips, popcorn, etc). We might have used one for a single bag of snacks and coffee. I suspect this would buy as less today. Hopefully the payout is bigger at airports like SFO, otherwise, AAs premium pitch is going to fall flat (don’t worry, we have more delays than the other majors, but don’t worry, when it happens, we’ll give you a voucher that covers fewer hotels than before, and a ‘food voucher’ that we renamed so you don’t get the impression that it would actually cover a meal – thanks for flying AA’

On a recent trip through Chicago O’Hare International Airport (ORD), I missed my connecting flight to the East Coast. Unless American Airlines (AA) somehow anticipated that my connecting flight would depart more than two hours late, the airline knew well in advance of my arrival at ORD, that I was likely to be stranded at ORD.

To make matters worse, my arrival at ORD was already more than two hours behind schedule because AA had knowingly oversold my original flight and apparently had to beg, borrow, and steal to get approximately 20 passengers off the flight so that it could depart. Given these circumstances, I would have expected AA to proactively make arrangements for displaced passengers, including securing hotel accommodations for those who would inevitably miss their connections.

Instead, when I approached the AA agents at ORD to request a hotel room, they appeared genuinely surprised by my request. Eventually, an agent provided me with a hotel voucher, round-trip taxi vouchers for transportation between the airport and a Courtyard by Marriott approximately 20 minutes away, and a nominal credit for food and beverages.

I find it difficult to believe that the deplorable establishment to which AA sent me was actually operating under the Courtyard by Marriott name. The hotel with which AA apparently has a contractual arrangement to accommodate stranded passengers was filthy, disgusting, and wholly unacceptable. It resembled a seedy, hourly-rate establishment far more than a Marriott-branded hotel. Frankly, it was a place I wouldn’t send my dog. I cannot imagine what AA was thinking when it selected this property to accommodate its passengers.

And the experience didn’t end there. Not a single taxi in the ORD taxi queue would accept AA’s taxi voucher. The same thing happened when I attempted to return to the airport. In other words, even the transportation arrangements AA provided were effectively useless, leaving me to deal with yet another completely unnecessary problem.

The entire experience was appalling. From the oversold originating flight and the resulting missed connection to the unacceptable hotel accommodations and worthless taxi vouchers, AA demonstrated a remarkable disregard for the passengers who depend on it.

I would expect American Airlines to treat a dog better than it treated me. Perhaps, however, in AA’s eyes, paying passengers have been relegated to little more than a nuisance.

That is certainly how I was made to feel.

As its air business softens, MakeMyTrip is pushing harder into everything else. Quick Ride gives it a product people use on a random Thursday, not just before a holiday. The test is whether those commuters become MakeMyTrip travelers.

MakeMyTrip Friday announced the acquisition of a majority stake in Bengaluru-based ride-pooling platform Quick Ride, expanding its ground transportation business.

The online travel company said the acquisition gives it an entry into the shared mobility segment, complementing its existing ground transport offerings, which include bus bookings through redBus and intercity car rentals through Savaari. MakeMyTrip did not say how much it invested in Quick Ride, or its precise ownership, beyond now holding a majority share.

Quick Ride connects commuters traveling along similar routes, allowing them to share rides and split commuting costs. The platform also works with corporates, IT parks and business campuses, giving it access to a customer base beyond individual travelers.

MakeMyTrip has acquired a majority stake in Bengaluru-based ride-pooling platform Quick Ride, adding daily urban commuting to a ground transport business that already includes redBus for buses and Savaari for intercity car rentals. The company did not disclose the price or its precise ownership level. Quick Ride moved its ride-pooling business and brand into a new entity, Co Ride Mobility, which MakeMyTrip now controls, while the electric vehicle taxi business stays with iDisha Info Labs and Quick Ride's existing promoters continue to run the business. The deal continues a run of acquisitions — Savaari in 2023, corporate expense platform Happay in 2024, Flamingo Transworld in group holidays, and a minority stake in visa processor Atlys — as MakeMyTrip pushes beyond flights and hotels ahead of a reported India IPO. The timing tracks with its results: non-air businesses reached 63.2% of gross bookings in the fiscal second quarter ended September 30, 2026, up from 61.5% a year earlier, and the "other" segment that includes cabs, insurance, foreign exchange, and activities posted adjusted margins of $24.4 million, up about 30% year over year. Ride-pooling gives MakeMyTrip something its other products do not: a reason for customers to open the app on days they are not traveling.

Nowadays, tech is everywhere when we travel, from power banks and portable fans to smart suitcases that follow their owners around the airport. But many of these devices come with a hidden risk.

In October, a British Airways flight was forced to make an emergency landing after a battery fire burned one of the passengers — and this is hardly an isolated incident. The Federal Aviation Administration reported 28 battery fire events on passenger and cargo planes in the first quarter of 2026 alone. That’s on track to beat last year’s tally of 97 events, up from 89 in 2024.

Fires can be particularly dangerous in the enclosed space of an airplane, so it’s critical for passengers to do their part by packing batteries correctly. Here’s an overview of the types of batteries you need to watch out for, what devices they’re in and how to pack them safely and legally.

Any battery can start a fire if stored improperly, but the biggest threats are lithium metal (non-rechargeable) and lithium-ion (rechargeable) batteries. These batteries have exploded in popularity in recent years. Unfortunately, they are also at risk of, quite literally, exploding.

According to the FAA, “All lithium-ion batteries are capable of overheating and experiencing a process called thermal runaway.”

Thermal runaway is a self-sustaining chemical reaction that produces extreme heat (up to 1,500 degrees F within seconds), toxic smoke, ultrafine particles and flames. It can occur without warning due to various factors, including damage to the battery, overheating, overcharging, exposure to water and manufacturing defects.

Lithium battery fires are often resistant to traditional extinguishing agents, making them tough for cabin crews to tackle. And since planes recirculate air rather than drawing fresh air from outside, toxic fumes from lithium fires can pose a health hazard to passengers long after the flames are extinguished.

As a result, the aviation industry has been tightening the rules on lithium batteries.

The most common culprits behind aircraft fires are cell phones, laptops, vapes and power banks. For example, three passengers were injured when a laptop battery caught fire on an American Airlines plane in 2024, and a power bank caused a similar emergency on a Virgin Australia flight in 2025.

However, lots of other devices can contain lithium batteries, such as:

To determine whether your device has a lithium battery, check the label or manual. The chemical symbol “Li” generally indicates the presence of lithium; you may see terms such as "Li-polymer," "LiPo” or "Li+." For coin-cell batteries, the label will typically start with “CR” if lithium is involved.

As you can see, there’s a good reason for all the restrictions around batteries on planes — but they can be confusing. If you’ve ever wondered how you should store your camera battery or whether you can pack that portable fan in your checked luggage, you’ve come to the right place.

Here, I’ll answer all of your, ahem, burning questions about batteries.

The regulations around lithium batteries depend on the battery size and whether they are alone or installed in a device.

Non-rechargeable batteries are limited to 2 grams of lithium per battery, while rechargeable batteries are limited to a rating of 100 watt hours. According to TSA, this covers “nearly all types of lithium batteries used by the average person in their electronic devices.” Larger batteries require approval from the airline.

TSA prohibits spare or uninstalled lithium batteries — which include power banks and cell phone charging cases — in checked baggage. These batteries must go in your carryon, and if you end up gate-checking your bag, you must remove them and keep them with you during the flight.

For lithium batteries contained within a device, you can pack them in your checked bag as long as the device is fully powered off and “protected from accidental activation,” according to the FAA. For devices that generate extreme heat (such as lighters), you must protect the device from switching on inside your checked bag by removing the battery or heating element.

Your specific airline may have additional rules regarding lithium batteries. For instance, Southwest has one of the strictest battery policies in the sky: Passengers are limited to one power bank per person, batteries are prohibited in overhead bins and they must be visible while in use.

The above guidelines apply only to lithium batteries. “Dry” batteries, such as AAs, button cells and 9-volts, are allowed in both checked and carry-on bags.

However, FAA guidelines state that “Battery terminals (usually the ends) must be protected from short circuit (i.e., the terminals must not come in contact with other metal).” You can keep your batteries safe by storing them in their original packaging, a battery case, the battery pocket of a camera bag or a plastic baggy. However, the FAA does not recommend packing rechargeable batteries in their charging unit.

Carrying lithium batteries onboard with you won’t prevent them from catching fire, but it will make it easier for flight crews to respond to any incidents. You can do your part by following these guidelines:

Baggage regulations can be tricky, but it’s worth paying attention. Passengers who don’t follow the rules can be slapped with serious fines — and, more importantly, they pose a safety hazard to everyone on their flight.

Follow the packing tips above to travel safely and stress-free, and check out our other travel safety tips:

#6130. Trans Thai Women Stole Tourist’s $600,000 Watch Over $60 Dispute—They ‘Thought It Was Fake’

A Chinese tourist says two women took his diamond-covered Patek Philippe and passport from his Pattaya hotel room. He valued the watch at roughly $600,000. When they demanded about $600 to return his belongings, he paid but only got his passport back. Police recovered the watch and arrested two suspects early Sunday morning. The suspects told police they were owed 2,000 baht (~ $60) and thought the watch was fake. The tourist reported the theft November 7 from room 309 at the Z8 Hotel. He said two transgender women took the watch and passport, then demanded 20,000 baht to return them. After collecting the cash, they returned the passport and left with the watch. The silver-colored, diamond-set Patek Philippe PP5719G can actually list at $725,000. The two suspects were arrested early in the morning of November 8. They claimed they’d just taken the watch figuring it was worth what they were owed (what they were owed for you can leave to your imagination). I’ve written about a guest who arrived at a Marriott wearing a $24,000 Rolex but hadn’t booked the night of his arrival. He fell asleep in the lobby waiting for a room, and someone took it right off his wrist. And in the stranger hotel watch recovery, two Rolexes taken from guests at Encore Las Vegas were concealed inside the women who stole them. A reader’s response to that story evokes Pulp Fiction: I don’t think I would ever wear the watch again. There is not enough disinfectant in the world. Now I can’t get images of the thieves looking just like Christopher Walken out of my mind. Y’all be careful on your travels out there! #6127. Wynn Holds UAE Casino Date but Weighs How to Open Amid War

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: A render of Wynn Al Marjan Island. Wynn Resorts

Wynn is holding to its September 2027 date for the UAE’s first casino resort but it will now decide in February what form the opening takes. The U.S.-Iran war means its first customers may travel from down the road in Dubai and elsewhere in the UAE, rather than being the international guests it primarily wants.

Casino resort operator Wynn Resorts will likely decide in February precisely how to open its Ras Al Khaimah casino resort, CEO Craig Billings said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call on Thursday.

“We will make a decision about the format in which we open. And we’ll probably make that decision around February,” he said.

The $5.7 billion Wynn Al Marjan Island, the UAE’s first integrated gaming resort, remains scheduled for an opening in September 2027. But Billings said the mix of source markets it ideally wants “does impact how we open.” He said that Wynn had “the playbooks for every single iteration of that today.”

Back in August, Wynn said it did not plan a staggered rollout. “We generally don’t do phased openings,” Billings then said. “We would open the doors and open all the amenities exactly as we would any other particular opening.”
